text: "...[T]he powers of financial capitalism had another far-reaching aim, nothing less than to create a world system of financial control in private hands able to dominate the political system of each country and the economy of the world as a whole, this system was to be controlled in a feudalist fashion by the central banks of the world acting in concert by secret agreements arrived at in frequent private meetings and conferences.
text_raw:
"...[T]he  powers  of  financial  capitalism  had  another  far-reaching  aim,  nothing  less
than  to  create  a  world  system  of  financial  control  in  private  hands  able  to  dominate  the
political  system  of  each  country  and  the  economy  of  the  world  as  a  whole,  this  system
was  to  be  controlled  in  a  feudalist  fashion  by  the  central  banks  of  the  world  acting  in
concert  by  secret  agreements  arrived  at  in  frequent  private  meetings  and  conferences.

text: The apex of the system was to be the Bank for International Settlements in Basle, Switzerland, a private bank owned and controlled by the world's central banks which were themselves private corporations....
text_raw:
The
apex  of  the  system  was  to  be  the  Bank  for  International  Settlements  in  Basle,
Switzerland,  a  private  bank  owned  and  controlled  by  the  world's  central  banks  which
were  themselves  private  corporations....

text: "It must not be felt that these heads of the world's chief central banks were themselves substantive powers in world finance.

text: The substantive financial powers of the world were in the hands of these investment bankers (also called 'international' or 'merchant' bankers) who remained largely behind the scenes in their own unincorporated private banks.

text: These formed a system of international cooperation and national dominance which was more private, more powerful, and more secret than that of their agents in the central banks, this dominance of investment bankers was based on their control over the flows of credit and investment funds in their own countries and throughout the world.

text: They could dominate the financial and industrial systems of their own countries by their influence over the flow of current funds though bank loans, the discount rate, and the re-discounting of commercial debts; they could dominate governments by their own control over current government loans and the play of the international exchanges.

text: Almost all of this power was exercised by the personal influence and prestige of men who had demonstrated their ability in the past to bring off successful financial coupes, to keep their word, to remain cool in a crisis, and to share their winning opportunities with their associates."

text: The result of all this, I hope, is an interpretation of the present as well as the immediate past and the near future, which is free from the accepted cliches, slogans, and self -justifications which mar so much of "contemporary history." This  change  is  evident  in  a  number  of  obvious  events,

text: Much more important is the fact that the Cold War, which culminated in the Cuban crisis of October 1962, began to dwindle toward its end during the next two years, a process which w as evident in a number of events, such as the rapid replacement of the Cold War by "Competitive Coexistence"; the disintegration of the two super-blocs which had faced each other during the Cold War; the rise of neutralism, both within the super-blocs and in the buffer fringe of third-bloc powers between them; the swamping of the United Nations General Assembly under a flood of newly independent, sometimes microscopic, pseudo-powers; the growing parallelism of the Soviet Union and the United States; and the growing emphasis in all parts of the world on problems of living standards, of social maladjustments, and of mental health, replacing the previous emphasis on armaments, nuclear tensions, and heavy industrialization.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: After the long years of the Age of Expansion, people's minds and their social organizations are adjusted to expansion, and it is a very difficult thing to readjust these to a decreasing rate of expansion.

After  the  long  years  of  the  Age  of  Expansion,
people's  minds  and  their  social  organizations  are  adjusted  to  expansion,  and  it  is  a  very
difficult  thing  to  readjust  these  to  a  decreasing  rate  of  expansion.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: Social classes and political units within the civilization try to compensate for the slowing of expansion through normal growth by the use of violence against other social classes or against other political units.

political  units  within  the  civilization  try  to  compensate  for  the  slowing  of  expansion

political  units.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: From this come class struggles and imperialist wars.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: The outcomes of these struggles within the civilization are not of vital significance for the future of the civilization itself.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: What would be of such significance would be the reorganization of the structure of the civilization so that the process of normal growth would be resumed.

What  would  be  of  such  significance  would  be  the  reorganization  of  the
structure  of  the  civilization  so  that  the  process  of  normal  growth  would  be  resumed.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: Because such a reorganization requires the removal of the causes of the civilization's decline, the triumph of one social class over another or of one political unit over another, within the civilization, will not usually have any major influence on the causes of the decline, and will not (except by accident) result in such a reorganization of structure as will give rise to a new period of expansion.

Because  such  a  reorganization  requires  the  removal  of  the  causes  of  the  civilization's

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: One cause, although by no means the chief cause, of the ability of Western Civilization to destroy other cultures rests on the fact that it has been expanding for a long time.
text_raw:
One  cause,  although  by  no  means  the  chief  cause,  of  the  ability  of  Western
Civilization  to  destroy  other  cultures  rests  on  the  fact  that  it  has  been  expanding  for  a
long  time.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: This fact, in turn, rests on another condition to which we have already alluded, the fact that Western Civilization has passed through three periods of expansion, has entered into an Age of Conflict three times, each time has had its core area conquered almost completely by a single political unit, but has failed to go on to the Age of the Universal Empire because from the confusion of the Age of Conflict there emerged each time a new organization of society capable of expanding by its own organizational powers, with the result that the four phenomena characteristic of the Age of Conflict (decreasing rate of expansion, class conflicts, imperialist wars, irrationality) were gradually replaced once again by the four kinds of expansion typical of an Age of Expansion (demographic, geographic, production, knowledge).
text_raw:
This  fact,  in  turn,  rests  on  another  condition  to  which  we  have  already  alluded,
the  fact  that  Western  Civilization  has  passed  through  three  periods  of  expansion,  has
entered  into  an  Age  of  Conflict  three  times,  each  time  has  had  its  core  area  conquered
almost  completely  by  a  single  political  unit,  but  has  failed  to  go  on  to  the  Age  of  the
Universal  Empire  because  from  the  confusion  of  the  Age  of  Conflict  there  emerged  each
time  a  new  organization  of  society  capable  of  expanding  by  its  own  organizational
powers,  with  the  result  that  the  four  phenomena  characteristic  of  the  Age  of  Conflict
(decreasing  rate  of  expansion,  class  conflicts,  imperialist  wars,  irrationality)  were
gradually  replaced  once  again  by  the  four  kinds  of  expansion  typical  of  an  Age  of
Expansion  (demographic,  geographic,  production,  knowledge).

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: From a narrowly technical point of view, this shift from an Age of Conflict to an Age of Expansion is marked by a resumption of the investment of capital and the accumulation of capital on a large scale, just as the earlier shift from the Age of Expansion to the Age of Conflict was marked by a decreasing rate of investment and eventually by a decreasing rate of accumulation of capital.
text_raw:
From  a  narrowly
technical  point  of  view,  this  shift  from  an  Age  of  Conflict  to  an  Age  of  Expansion  is
marked  by  a  resumption  of  the  investment  of  capital  and  the  accumulation  of  capital  on  a
large  scale,  just  as  the  earlier  shift  from  the  Age  of  Expansion  to  the  Age  of  Conflict  was
marked  by  a  decreasing  rate  of  investment  and  eventually  by  a  decreasing  rate  of
accumulation  of  capital.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: Western Civilization began, as all civilizations do, in a period of cultural mixture.
text_raw: Western  Civilization  began,  as  all  civilizations  do,  in  a  period  of  cultural  mixture.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: In this particular case it was a mixture resulting from the barbarian invasions which destroyed Classical Civilization in the period 350-700.
text_raw:
In
this  particular  case  it  was  a  mixture  resulting  from  the  barbarian  invasions  which
destroyed  Classical  Civilization  in  the  period  350-700.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: By creating a new culture from the various elements offered from the barbarian tribes, the Roman world, the Saracen world, and above all the Jewish world (Christianity), Western Civilization became a new society.
text_raw:
By  creating  a  new  culture  from
the  various  elements  offered  from  the  barbarian  tribes,  the  Roman  world,  the  Saracen
world,  and  above  all  the  Jewish  world  (Christianity),  Western  Civilization  became  a  new
society.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: This society became a civilization when it became organized, in the period 700-970, so that there was accumulation of capital and the beginnings of the investment of this capital in new methods of production.
text_raw:
This  society  became  a  civilization  when  it  became  organized,  in  the  period  700-970,
so  that  there  was  accumulation  of  capital  and  the  beginnings  of  the  investment  of  this
capital  in  new  methods  of  production.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: These new methods are associated with a change from infantry forces to mounted warriors in defense, from manpower (and thus slavery) to animal power in energy use, from the scratch plow and two-field, fallow agricultural technology of Mediterranean Europe to the eight-oxen, gang plow and three-field system of the Germanic peoples, and from the centralized, state-centered political orientation of the Roman world to the decentralized, private-power feudal network of the medieval world.
text_raw:
These  new  methods  are  associated  with  a  change
from  infantry  forces  to  mounted  warriors  in  defense,  from  manpower  (and  thus  slavery)
to  animal  power  in  energy  use,  from  the  scratch  plow  and  two-field,  fallow  agricultural
technology  of  Mediterranean  Europe  to  the  eight-oxen,  gang  plow  and  three-field  system
of  the  Germanic  peoples,  and  from  the  centralized,  state-centered  political  orientation  of
the  Roman  world  to  the  decentralized,  private-power  feudal  network  of  the  medieval
world.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: In the new system a small number of men, equipped and trained to fight, received dues and services from the overwhelming majority of men who were expected to till the soil.
text_raw:
In  the  new  system  a  small  number  of  men,  equipped  and  trained  to  fight,  received
dues  and  services  from  the  overwhelming  majority  of  men  who  were  expected  to  till  the
soil.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: From this inequitable but effective defensive system emerged an inequitable distribution of political power and, in turn, an inequitable distribution of the social economic income.
text_raw:
From  this  inequitable  but  effective  defensive  system  emerged  an  inequitable
distribution  of  political  power  and,  in  turn,  an  inequitable  distribution  of  the  social
economic  income.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: This, in time, resulted in an accumulation of capital, which, by giving rise to demand for luxury goods of remote origin, began to shift the whole economic emphasis of the society from its earlier organization in self-sufficient agrarian units (manors) to commercial interchange, economic specialization, and, by the thirteenth century, to an entirely new pattern of society with towns, a bourgeois class, spreading literacy, growing freedom of alternative social choices, and new, often disturbing, thoughts.
text_raw:
This,  in  time,  resulted  in  an  accumulation  of  capital,  which,  by  giving
rise  to  demand  for  luxury  goods  of  remote  origin,  began  to  shift  the  whole  economic
emphasis  of  the  society  from  its  earlier  organization  in  self-sufficient  agrarian  units
(manors)  to  commercial  interchange,  economic  specialization,  and,  by  the  thirteenth
century,  to  an  entirely  new  pattern  of  society  with  towns,  a  bourgeois  class,  spreading
literacy,  growing  freedom  of  alternative  social  choices,  and  new,  often  disturbing,
thoughts.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: From all this came the first period of expansion of Western Civilization, covering the years 970-1270.
text_raw:
From  all  this  came  the  first  period  of  expansion  of  Western  Civilization,  covering  the
years  970-1270.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: At the end of this period, the organization of society was becoming a petrified collection of vested interests, investment was decreasing, and the rate of expansion was beginning to fall.
text_raw:
At  the  end  of  this  period,  the  organization  of  society  was  becoming  a
petrified  collection  of  vested  interests,  investment  was  decreasing,  and  the  rate  of
expansion  was  beginning  to  fall.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: Accordingly, Western Civilization, for the first time, entered upon the Age of Conflict.
text_raw:
Accordingly,  Western  Civilization,  for  the  first  time,
entered  upon  the  Age  of  Conflict.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: This period, the time of the Hundred Years' War, the Black Death, the great heresies, and severe class conflicts, lasted from about 1270 to 1420.
text_raw:
This  period,  the  time  of  the  Hundred  Years'  War,  the
Black  Death,  the  great  heresies,  and  severe  class  conflicts,  lasted  from  about  1270  to
1420.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: By the end of it, efforts were arising from England and Burgundy to conquer the eve of Western Civilization.
text_raw:
By  the  end  of  it,  efforts  were  arising  from  England  and  Burgundy  to  conquer  the
eve  of  Western  Civilization.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: But, just at that moment, a new Age of Expansion, using a new organization of society which circumvented the old vested interests of the feudal- manorial system, began.
text_raw:
But,  just  at  that  moment,  a  new  Age  of  Expansion,  using  a
new  organization  of  society  which  circumvented  the  old  vested  interests  of  the  feudal-
manorial  system,  began.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: This new Age of Expansion, frequently called the period of commercial capitalism, lasted from about 1440 to about 1680.
text_raw:
This  new  Age  of  Expansion,  frequently  called  the  period  of  commercial  capitalism,
lasted  from  about  1440  to  about  1680.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: The real impetus to economic expansion during the period came from efforts to obtain profits by the interchange of goods, especially semi-luxury or luxury goods, over long distances.
text_raw:
The  real  impetus  to  economic  expansion  during
the  period  came  from  efforts  to  obtain  profits  by  the  interchange  of  goods,  especially
semi-luxury  or  luxury  goods,  over  long  distances.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: In time, this system of commercial capitalism became petrified into a structure of vested interests in which profits were sought by imposing restrictions on the production or interchange of goods rather than by encouraging these activities.
text_raw:
In  time,  this  system  of  commercial
capitalism  became  petrified  into  a  structure  of  vested  interests  in  which  profits  were
sought  by  imposing  restrictions  on  the  production  or  interchange  of  goods  rather  than  by
encouraging  these  activities.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: This new vested-interest structure, usually called mercantilism, became such a burden on economic activities that the rate of expansion of
text_raw:
This  new  vested-interest  structure,  usually  called
mercantilism,  became  such  a  burden  on  economic  activities  that  the  rate  of  expansion  of

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: economic life declined and even gave rise to a period of economic decline in the decades immediately following 1690.
text_raw:
economic  life  declined  and  even  gave  rise  to  a  period  of  economic  decline  in  the  decades
immediately  following  1690.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: The class struggles and imperialist wars engendered by this Age of Conflict are sometimes called the Second Hundred Years' War.
text_raw:
The  class  struggles  and  imperialist  wars  engendered  by  this
Age  of  Conflict  are  sometimes  called  the  Second  Hundred  Years'  War.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: The wars continued until 1815, and the class struggles even later.
text_raw:
The  wars
continued  until  1815,  and  the  class  struggles  even  later.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: As a result of the former, France by 1810 had conquered most of the eve of Western Civilization.
text_raw:
As  a  result  of  the  former,  France
by  1810  had  conquered  most  of  the  eve  of  Western  Civilization.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: But here, just as had occurred in 1420 when England had also conquered part of the core of the civilization toward the latter portion of an Age of Conflict, the victory was made meaningless because a new period of expansion began.
text_raw:
But  here,  just  as  had
occurred  in  1420  when  England  had  also  conquered  part  of  the  core  of  the  civilization
toward  the  latter  portion  of  an  Age  of  Conflict,  the  victory  was  made  meaningless
because  a  new  period  of  expansion  began.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: Just as commercial capitalism had circumvented the petrified institution of the feudal-manorial system (chivalry) after 1440, so industrial capitalism circumvented the petrified institution of commercial capitalism (mercantilism) after 1820.
text_raw:
Just  as  commercial  capitalism  had
circumvented  the  petrified  institution  of  the  feudal-manorial  system  (chivalry)  after  1440,
so  industrial  capitalism  circumvented  the  petrified  institution  of  commercial  capitalism
(mercantilism)  after  1820.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: The new Age of Expansion which made Napoleon's military-political victory of 1810 impossible to maintain had begun in England long before.
text_raw:
The  new  Age  of  Expansion  which  made  Napoleon's  military-political  victory  of  1810
impossible  to  maintain  had  begun  in  England  long  before.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: It appeared as the Agricultural Revolution about 1725 and as the Industrial Revolution about 1775, but it did not get started as a great burst of expansion until after 1820.
text_raw:
It  appeared  as  the  Agricultural
Revolution  about  1725  and  as  the  Industrial  Revolution  about  1775,  but  it  did  not  get
started  as  a  great  burst  of  expansion  until  after  1820.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: Once started, it moved forward with an impetus such as the world had never seen before, and it looked as if Western Civilization might cover the whole globe.
text_raw:
Once  started,  it  moved  forward  with
an  impetus  such  as  the  world  had  never  seen  before,  and  it  looked  as  if  Western
Civilization  might  cover  the  whole  globe.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: The dates of this third Age of Expansion might be fixed at 1770-1929, following upon the second Age of Conflict of 1690-1815.
text_raw:
The  dates  of  this  third  Age  of  Expansion  might
be  fixed  at  1770-1929,  following  upon  the  second  Age  of  Conflict  of  1690-1815.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: The social organization which was at the center of this new development might be called "industrial capitalism." In the course of the last decade of the nineteenth century, it began to become a structure of vested interests to which we might give the name "monopoly capitalism." As early, perhaps, as 1890, certain aspects of a new Age of Conflict, the third in Western Civilization, began to appear, especially in the core area, with a revival of imperialism, of class struggle, of violent warfare, and of irrationalities.
text_raw:
The
social  organization  which  was  at  the  center  of  this  new  development  might  be  called
"industrial  capitalism."  In  the  course  of  the  last  decade  of  the  nineteenth  century,  it  began
to  become  a  structure  of  vested  interests  to  which  we  might  give  the  name  "monopoly
capitalism."  As  early,  perhaps,  as  1890,  certain  aspects  of  a  new  Age  of  Conflict,  the
third  in  Western  Civilization,  began  to  appear,  especially  in  the  core  area,  with  a  revival
of  imperialism,  of  class  struggle,  of  violent  warfare,  and  of  irrationalities.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: By 1930 it was clear that Western Civilization was again in an Age of Conflict; by 1942 a semi -peripheral state, Germany, had conquered much of the core of the civilization.
text_raw:
By  1930  it  was  clear  that  Western  Civilization  was  again  in  an  Age  of  Conflict;  by
1942  a  semi -peripheral  state,  Germany,  had  conquered  much  of  the  core  of  the
civilization.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: That effort was defeated by calling into the fray a peripheral state (the United States) and another, outside civilization (the Soviet society).
text_raw:
That  effort  was  defeated  by  calling  into  the  fray  a  peripheral  state  (the  United
States)  and  another,  outside  civilization  (the  Soviet  society).

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: It is not yet clear whether Western Civilization will continue along the path marked by so many earlier civilizations, or whether it will be able to reorganize itself sufficiently to enter upon a new, fourth, Age of Expansion.
text_raw:
It  is  not  yet  clear  whether
Western  Civilization  will  continue  along  the  path  marked  by  so  many  earlier

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: During much of the last four hundred years culminating in the twentieth century, the fringes of Asia have been occupied by a semicircle of old dying civilizations (Islamic, Hindu, Chinese, Japanese).
text_raw:
During  much  of  the  last  four  hundred  years  culminating  in  the
twentieth  century,  the  fringes  of  Asia  have  been  occupied  by  a  semicircle  of  old  dying
civilizations  (Islamic,  Hindu,  Chinese,  Japanese).

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: These have been under pressure from Western Civilization coming in from the oceans and from Orthodox Civilization pushing outward from the heart of the Eurasian land mass.
text_raw:
These  have  been  under  pressure  from
Western  Civilization  coming  in  from  the  oceans  and  from  Orthodox  Civilization  pushing
outward  from  the  heart  of  the  Eurasian  land  mass.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: The Oceanic pressure began with Vasco da Gama in India in 1498, culminated aboard the battleship Missouri in Tokyo Bay in 1945, and still continued with the Anglo-French attack on Suez in 1956.
text_raw:
The  Oceanic  pressure  began  with
Vasco  da  Gama  in  India  in  1498,  culminated  aboard  the  battleship  Missouri  in  Tokyo
Bay  in  1945,  and  still  continued  with  the  Anglo-French  attack  on  Suez  in  1956.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: The Russian pressure from the continental heartland was applied to the inner frontiers of China, Iran, and Turkey from the seventeenth century to the present.
text_raw:
The
Russian  pressure  from  the  continental  heartland  was  applied  to  the  inner  frontiers  of
China,  Iran,  and  Turkey  from  the  seventeenth  century  to  the  present.

chapter_title: Chapter  1 â€” Cultural  Evolution  in  Civilizations
text: Much of the world's history in the twentieth century has arisen from the interactions of these three factors (the continental heartland of Russian power, the shattered cultures of the Buffer Fringe of Asia, and the oceanic powers of Western Civilization).
text_raw:
Much  of  the  world's
history  in  the  twentieth  century  has  arisen  from  the  interactions  of  these  three  factors  (the
continental  heartland  of  Russian  power,  the  shattered  cultures  of  the  Buffer  Fringe  of
Asia,  and  the  oceanic  powers  of  Western  Civilization).

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: We have said that the culture of a civilization is created in its core area originally and moves outward into peripheral areas which thus become part of the civilization.
text_raw:
We  have  said  that  the  culture  of  a  civilization  is  created  in  its  core  area  originally  and
moves  outward  into  peripheral  areas  which  thus  become  part  of  the  civilization.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: This movement of cultural elements is called "diffusion" by students of the subject.
text_raw:
This
movement  of  cultural  elements  is  called  "diffusion"  by  students  of  the  subject.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: It is noteworthy that material elements of a culture, such as tools, weapons, vehicles, and such, diffuse more readily and thus more rapidly than do the nonmaterial elements such as ideas, art forms, religious outlook, or patterns of social behavior.
text_raw:
It  is
noteworthy  that  material  elements  of  a  culture,  such  as  tools,  weapons,  vehicles,  and
such,  diffuse  more  readily  and  thus  more  rapidly  than  do  the  nonmaterial  elements  such
as  ideas,  art  forms,  religious  outlook,  or  patterns  of  social  behavior.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: For this reason the peripheral portions of a civilization (such as Assyria in Mesopotamian Civilization, Rome or Spain in Classical Civilization, and the United States or Australia in Western Civilization) tend to have a somewhat cruder and more material culture than the core area of the same civilization.
text_raw:
For  this  reason  the
peripheral  portions  of  a  civilization  (such  as  Assyria  in  Mesopotamian  Civilization,  Rome
or  Spain  in  Classical  Civilization,  and  the  United  States  or  Australia  in  Western
Civilization)  tend  to  have  a  somewhat  cruder  and  more  material  culture  than  the  core  area
of  the  same  civilization.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: Material elements of a culture also diffuse beyond the boundaries of a civilization into other societies, and do so much more readily than the nonmaterial elements of the culture.
text_raw:
Material  elements  of  a  culture  also  diffuse  beyond  the  boundaries  of  a  civilization  into
other  societies,  and  do  so  much  more  readily  than  the  nonmaterial  elements  of  the  culture.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: For this reason the nonmaterial and spiritual elements of a culture are what give it its distinctive character rather than its tools and weapons which can be so easily exported to entirely different societies.
text_raw:
For  this  reason  the  nonmaterial  and  spiritual  elements  of  a  culture  are  what  give  it  its
distinctive  character  rather  than  its  tools  and  weapons  which  can  be  so  easily  exported  to
entirely  different  societies.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: Thus, the distinctive character of Western Civilization rests on its Christian heritage, its scientific outlook, its humanitarian elements, and its distinctive point of view in regard to the rights of the individual and respect for women rather than in such material things as firearms, tractors, plumbing fixtures, or skyscrapers, all of which are exportable commodities.
text_raw:
Thus,  the  distinctive  character  of  Western  Civilization  rests  on
its  Christian  heritage,  its  scientific  outlook,  its  humanitarian  elements,  and  its  distinctive
point  of  view  in  regard  to  the  rights  of  the  individual  and  respect  for  women  rather  than
in  such  material  things  as  firearms,  tractors,  plumbing  fixtures,  or  skyscrapers,  all  of
which  are  exportable  commodities.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: The export of material elements in a culture, across its peripheral areas and beyond, to the peoples of totally different societies has strange results.
text_raw:
The  export  of  material  elements  in  a  culture,  across  its  peripheral  areas  and  beyond,  to
the  peoples  of  totally  different  societies  has  strange  results.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: As elements of material culture move from core to periphery inside a civilization, they tend, in the long run, to strengthen the periphery at the expense of the core because the core is more hampered in the use of material innovations by the strength of past vested interests and because the core devotes a much greater part of its wealth and energy to nonmaterial culture.
text_raw:
As  elements  of  material
culture  move  from  core  to  periphery  inside  a  civilization,  they  tend,  in  the  long  run,  to
strengthen  the  periphery  at  the  expense  of  the  core  because  the  core  is  more  hampered  in
the  use  of  material  innovations  by  the  strength  of  past  vested  interests  and  because  the
core  devotes  a  much  greater  part  of  its  wealth  and  energy  to  nonmaterial  culture.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: Thus, such aspects of the Industrial Revolution as automobiles and radios are European rather than American inventions, but have been developed and utilized to a far greater extent in America because this area was not hampered in their use by surviving elements of feudalism, of church domination, of rigid class distinctions (for example, in education), or by widespread attention to music, poetry, art, or religion such as we find in Europe.
text_raw:
Thus,
such  aspects  of  the  Industrial  Revolution  as  automobiles  and  radios  are  European  rather
than  American  inventions,  but  have  been  developed  and  utilized  to  a  far  greater  extent  in
America  because  this  area  was  not  hampered  in  their  use  by  surviving  elements  of
feudalism,  of  church  domination,  of  rigid  class  distinctions  (for  example,  in  education),
or  by  widespread  attention  to  music,  poetry,  art,  or  religion  such  as  we  find  in  Europe.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: A similar contrast can be seen in Classical Civilization between Greek and Roman or in Mesopotamian Civilization between Sumerian and Assyrian or in Mayan Civilization between Mayan and Aztec.
text_raw:
A
similar  contrast  can  be  seen  in  Classical  Civilization  between  Greek  and  Roman  or  in
Mesopotamian  Civilization  between  Sumerian  and  Assyrian  or  in  Mayan  Civilization
between  Mayan  and  Aztec.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: The diffusion of culture elements beyond the boundaries of one society into the culture of another society presents quite a different case.
text_raw:
The  diffusion  of  culture  elements  beyond  the  boundaries  of  one  society  into  the
culture  of  another  society  presents  quite  a  different  case.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: The boundaries between societies present relatively little hindrance to the diffusion of material elements, and relatively greater hindrance to the diffusion of nonmaterial elements.
text_raw:
The  boundaries  between
societies  present  relatively  little  hindrance  to  the  diffusion  of  material  elements,  and
relatively  greater  hindrance  to  the  diffusion  of  nonmaterial  elements.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: Indeed, it is this fact which determines the boundary of the society, for, if the nonmaterial elements also diffused, the new area into which they flowed would be a peripheral portion of the old society rather than a part of a quite different society.
text_raw:
Indeed,  it  is  this  fact
which  determines  the  boundary  of  the  society,  for,  if  the  nonmaterial  elements  also
diffused,  the  new  area  into  which  they  flowed  would  be  a  peripheral  portion  of  the  old
society  rather  than  a  part  of  a  quite  different  society.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: The diffusion of material elements from one society to another has a complex effect on the importing society.
text_raw:
The  diffusion  of  material  elements  from  one  society  to  another  has  a  complex  effect
on  the  importing  society.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: In the short run it is usually benefitted by the importation, but in the long run it is frequently disorganized and weakened.
text_raw:
In  the  short  run  it  is  usually  benefitted  by  the  importation,  but  in
the  long  run  it  is  frequently  disorganized  and  weakened.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: When white men first came to North America, material elements from Western Civilization spread rapidly among the different Indian tribes.
text_raw:
When  white  men  first  came  to
North  America,  material  elements  from  Western  Civilization  spread  rapidly  among  the
different  Indian  tribes.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: The Plains Indians, for example, were weak and impoverished before 1543, but in that year the horse began to diffuse northward from the Spaniards in Mexico.
text_raw:
The  Plains  Indians,  for  example,  were  weak  and  impoverished
before  1543,  but  in  that  year  the  horse  began  to  diffuse  northward  from  the  Spaniards  in
Mexico.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: Within a century the Plains Indians were raised to a much higher standard of living (because of ability to hunt buffalo from horseback) and were immensely strengthened in their ability to resist Americans coming westward across the continent.
text_raw:
Within  a  century  the  Plains  Indians  were  raised  to  a  much  higher  standard  of
living  (because  of  ability  to  hunt  buffalo  from  horseback)  and  were  immensely
strengthened  in  their  ability  to  resist  Americans  coming  westward  across  the  continent.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: In the meantime, the trans-Appalachian Indians who had been very powerful in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries began to receive firearms, steel traps, measles, and eventually whiskey from the French and later the English by way of the St. Lawrence.
text_raw:
In
the  meantime,  the  trans-Appalachian  Indians  who  had  been  very  powerful  in  the  sixteenth
and  early  seventeenth  centuries  began  to  receive  firearms,  steel  traps,  measles,  and
eventually  whiskey  from  the  French  and  later  the  English  by  way  of  the  St.  Lawrence.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: These greatly weakened the woods Indians of the trans-Appalachian area and ultimately weakened the Plains Indians of the trans-Mississippi area, because measles and whiskey were devastating and demoralizing and because the use of traps and guns by certain tribes made them dependent on whites for supplies at the same time that they allowed them to put great physical pressure on the more remote tribes which had not yet received guns or traps.
text_raw:
These  greatly  weakened  the  woods  Indians  of  the  trans-Appalachian  area  and  ultimately
weakened  the  Plains  Indians  of  the  trans-Mississippi  area,  because  measles  and  whiskey
were  devastating  and  demoralizing  and  because  the  use  of  traps  and  guns  by  certain  tribes
made  them  dependent  on  whites  for  supplies  at  the  same  time  that  they  allowed  them  to
put  great  physical  pressure  on  the  more  remote  tribes  which  had  not  yet  received  guns  or
traps.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: Any united front of reds against whites was impossible, and the Indians were disrupted, demoralized, and destroyed.
text_raw:
Any  united  front  of  reds  against  whites  was  impossible,  and  the  Indians  were
disrupted,  demoralized,  and  destroyed.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: In general, importation of an element of material culture from one society to another is helpful to the importing society in the long run only if it is (a) productive, (b) can be made within the society itself, and (c) can be fitted into the nonmaterial culture of the importing society without demoralizing it.
text_raw:
In  general,  importation  of  an  element  of  material
culture  from  one  society  to  another  is  helpful  to  the  importing  society  in  the  long  run  only
if  it  is  (a)  productive,  (b)  can  be  made  within  the  society  itself,  and  (c)  can  be  fitted  into
the  nonmaterial  culture  of  the  importing  society  without  demoralizing  it.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: The destructive impact of Western Civilization upon so many other societies rests on its ability to
text_raw:
The  destructive
impact  of  Western  Civilization  upon  so  many  other  societies  rests  on  its  ability  to

text: As we shall see in a moment, many of the problems which the world faced at the middle of the twentieth century were rooted in the fact that these different aspects of the European way of life spread outward into the non-European world at such different speeds that the non-European world obtained them in an entirely different order from that in which Europe had obtained them.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization

text: This means that Europe was able to produce its own iron, steel, and copper to build its own railroads and telegraph wires, but the non-European world could construct these things only by obtaining the necessary industrial materials from Europe and thus becoming the debtor of Europe.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization
text: At this point the demographic cycle of an expanding population goes into a third stage (Population Type C) in which the birthrate also begins to fall.

text: The reasons for this fall in the birthrate have never been explained in a satisfactory way, but, as a consequence of it, there appears a new demographic condition marked by a falling birthrate, a low death rate, and a stabilizing and aging population whose major part is in the mature years from thirty to sixty.

text: It must be confessed that the nature of the fourth stage of this demographic cycle is based on theoretical considerations rather than on empirical observation, because even western Europe, where the cycle is most advanced, has not yet reached this fourth stage.

chapter_title: Chapter  2 â€” Cultural  Diffusion  in  Western  Civilization

text: As these two revolutions have diffused outward from western Europe to more peripheral areas of the world (the lifesaving revolution passing the food-producing revolution in the process), these more remote areas have entered, one by one, upon the demographic cycle.

text: But mass production required mass consumption so that the products of the new technology had to be distributed to the working groups as well as to others so that rising standards of living for the masses made the proletariat fewer and fewer and richer and richer.
text_raw:
But  mass
production  required  mass  consumption  so  that  the  products  of  the  new  technology  had  to
be  distributed  to  the  working  groups  as  well  as  to  others  so  that  rising  standards  of  living
for  the  masses  made  the  proletariat  fewer  and  fewer  and  richer  and  richer.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: At the same time, the need for managerial and white-collar workers of the middle levels of the economic system raised the proletariat into the middle class in large numbers.
text_raw:
At  the  same
time,  the  need  for  managerial  and  white-collar  workers  of  the  middle  levels  of  the
economic  system  raised  the  proletariat  into  the  middle  class  in  large  numbers.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: The spread of the corporate form of industrial enterprise allowed control to be separated from ownership and allowed the latter to be dispersed over a much wider group, so that, in effect, owners became more and more numerous and poorer and poorer.
text_raw:
The  spread
of  the  corporate  form  of  industrial  enterprise  allowed  control  to  be  separated  from
ownership  and  allowed  the  latter  to  be  dispersed  over  a  much  wider  group,  so  that,  in
effect,  owners  became  more  and  more  numerous  and  poorer  and  poorer.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: And, finally, control shifted from owners to managers.
text_raw:
And,  finally,
control  shifted  from  owners  to  managers.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: The result was that the polarized two-class society envisaged by Marx was, after 1900, increasingly replaced by a mass middle-class society, with fewer poor and, if not fewer rich, at least a more numerous group of rich who were relatively less rich than in an earlier period.
text_raw:
The  result  was  that  the  polarized  two-class
society  envisaged  by  Marx  was,  after  1900,  increasingly  replaced  by  a  mass  middle-class
society,  with  fewer  poor  and,  if  not  fewer  rich,  at  least  a  more  numerous  group  of  rich
who  were  relatively  less  rich  than  in  an  earlier  period.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: This process of leveling up the poor and leveling down the rich originated in economic forces but was speeded up and extended by governmental policies in regard to taxation and social welfare, especially after 1945.
text_raw:
This  process  of  leveling  up  the
poor  and  leveling  down  the  rich  originated  in  economic  forces  but  was  speeded  up  and
extended  by  governmental  policies  in  regard  to  taxation  and  social  welfare,  especially
after  1945.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: The Religious and Intellectual Stages of Culture
text_raw: The  Religious  and  Intellectual  Stages  of  Culture

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: When we turn to the higher levels of culture, such as the religious and intellectual aspects, we can discern a sequence of stages similar to those which have been found in the more material levels.
text_raw:
When  we  turn  to  the  higher  levels  of  culture,  such  as  the  religious  and  intellectual
aspects,  we  can  discern  a  sequence  of  stages  similar  to  those  which  have  been  found  in
the  more  material  levels.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: We shall make no extended examination of these at this time except to say that the religious level has seen a shift from a basically secularist, materialist, and antireligious outlook in the late nineteenth century to a much more spiritualist and religious point of view in the course of the twentieth century.
text_raw:
We  shall  make  no  extended  examination  of  these  at  this  time
except  to  say  that  the  religious  level  has  seen  a  shift  from  a  basically  secularist,
materialist,  and  antireligious  outlook  in  the  late  nineteenth  century  to  a  much  more
spiritualist  and  religious  point  of  view  in  the  course  of  the  twentieth  century.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: At the same time a very complex development on the intellectual level has shown a profound shift in outlook from an optimistic and scientific point of view in the period 1860-1890 to a much more pessimistic and irrationalist point of view in the period following 1890.
text_raw:
At  the  same
time  a  very  complex  development  on  the  intellectual  level  has  shown  a  profound  shift  in
outlook  from  an  optimistic  and  scientific  point  of  view  in  the  period  1860-1890  to  a  much
more  pessimistic  and  irrationalist  point  of  view  in  the  period  following  1890.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: This shift in point of view, which began in a rather restricted group forming an intellectual vanguard about 1890, a group which included such figures as Freud, Sorel, Bergson, and Proust, spread downward to larger and larger sections of Western society in the course of the new century as a result of the devastating experience of two world wars and the great depression.
text_raw:
This  shift  in
point  of  view,  which  began  in  a  rather  restricted  group  forming  an  intellectual  vanguard
about  1890,  a  group  which  included  such  figures  as  Freud,  Sorel,  Bergson,  and  Proust,
spread  downward  to  larger  and  larger  sections  of  Western  society  in  the  course  of  the
new  century  as  a  result  of  the  devastating  experience  of  two  world  wars  and  the  great
depression.

chapter_title: Chapter  4 â€” The  Pattern  of  Change
text: The results of this process can be seen in the striking contrast between the typical outlook of Europe in the nineteenth century and in the twentieth century as outlined in the preceding chapter.
text_raw:
The  results  of  this  process  can  be  seen  in  the  striking  contrast  between  the
typical  outlook  of  Europe  in  the  nineteenth  century  and  in  the  twentieth  century  as
outlined  in  the  preceding  chapter.

text: Commercial Capitalism
text_raw: Commercial  Capitalism

text: Western Civilization is the richest and most powerful social organization ever made by man.
text_raw:
Western  Civilization  is  the  richest  and  most  powerful  social  organization  ever  made
by  man.

text: One reason for this success has been its economic organization.
text_raw: One  reason  for  this  success  has  been  its  economic  organization.

text: This, as we have said, has passed through six successive stages, of which at least four are called "capitalism." Three features are notable about this development as a whole.
text_raw:
This,  as  we  have
said,  has  passed  through  six  successive  stages,  of  which  at  least  four  are  called
"capitalism."  Three  features  are  notable  about  this  development  as  a  whole.

text: In the first place, each stage crated the conditions which tended to bring about the next stage; therefore we could say, in a sense, that each stage committed suicide.
text_raw:
In  the  first  place,  each  stage  crated  the  conditions  which  tended  to  bring  about  the  next
stage;  therefore  we  could  say,  in  a  sense,  that  each  stage  committed  suicide.

text: The original economic organization of self-sufficient agrarian units (manors) was in a society organized so that its upper ranks â€” the lords, lay and ecclesiastical â€” found their desires for necessities so well met that they sought to exchange their surpluses of necessities for luxuries of remote origin.
text_raw:
The  original
economic  organization  of  self-sufficient  agrarian  units  (manors)  was  in  a  society
organized  so  that  its  upper  ranks â€” the  lords,  lay  and  ecclesiastical â€” found  their  desires
for  necessities  so  well  met  that  they  sought  to  exchange  their  surpluses  of  necessities  for
luxuries  of  remote  origin.

text: This gave rise to a trade in foreign luxuries (spices, fine textiles, fine metals) which was the first evidence of the stage of commercial capitalism.
text_raw:
This  gave  rise  to  a  trade  in  foreign  luxuries  (spices,  fine
textiles,  fine  metals)  which  was  the  first  evidence  of  the  stage  of  commercial  capitalism.

text: In this second stage, mercantile profits and widening markets created a demand for textiles and other goods which could be met only by application of power to production.
text_raw:
In  this  second  stage,  mercantile  profits  and  widening  markets  created  a  demand  for
textiles  and  other  goods  which  could  be  met  only  by  application  of  power  to  production.

text: This gave the third stage: industrial capitalism.
text_raw: This  gave  the  third  stage:  industrial  capitalism.

text: The stage of industrial capitalism soon gave rise to such an insatiable demand for heavy fixed capital, like railroad lines, steel mills, shipyards, and so on, that these investments could not be financed from the profits and private fortunes of individual proprietors.
text_raw:
The  stage  of  industrial  capitalism  soon
gave  rise  to  such  an  insatiable  demand  for  heavy  fixed  capital,  like  railroad  lines,  steel
mills,  shipyards,  and  so  on,  that  these  investments  could  not  be  financed  from  the  profits
and  private  fortunes  of  individual  proprietors.

text: New instruments for financing industry came into existence in the form of limited-liability corporations and investment banks.
text_raw:
New  instruments  for  financing  industry
came  into  existence  in  the  form  of  limited-liability  corporations  and  investment  banks.

text: These were soon in a position to control the chief parts of the industrial system, since they provided capital to it.
text_raw:
These  were  soon  in  a  position  to  control  the  chief  parts  of  the  industrial  system,  since
they  provided  capital  to  it.

text: This gave rise to financial capitalism.
text_raw: This  gave  rise  to  financial  capitalism.

text: The control of financial capitalism was used to integrate the industrial system into ever-larger units with interlinking financial controls.
text_raw:
The  control  of  financial
capitalism  was  used  to  integrate  the  industrial  system  into  ever-larger  units  with
interlinking  financial  controls.

text: This made possible a reduction of competition with a resulting increase in profits.
text_raw:
This  made  possible  a  reduction  of  competition  with  a
resulting  increase  in  profits.

text: As a result, the industrial system soon found that it was again able to finance its own expansion from its own profits, and, with this achievement, financial controls were weakened, and the stage of monopoly capitalism arrived.
text_raw:
As  a  result,  the  industrial  system  soon  found  that  it  was  again
able  to  finance  its  own  expansion  from  its  own  profits,  and,  with  this  achievement,
financial  controls  were  weakened,  and  the  stage  of  monopoly  capitalism  arrived.

text: In this fifth stage, great industrial units, working together either directly or through cartels and trade associations, were in a position to exploit the majority of the people.
text_raw:
In  this
fifth  stage,  great  industrial  units,  working  together  either  directly  or  through  cartels  and
trade  associations,  were  in  a  position  to  exploit  the  majority  of  the  people.

text: The result was a great economic crisis which soon developed into a struggle for control of the state â€” the minority hoping to use political power to defend their privileged position, the majority hoping to use the state to curtail the power and privileges of the minority.
text_raw:
The  result  was
a  great  economic  crisis  which  soon  developed  into  a  struggle  for  control  of  the  state â€” the
minority  hoping  to  use  political  power  to  defend  their  privileged  position,  the  majority
hoping  to  use  the  state  to  curtail  the  power  and  privileges  of  the  minority.

text: Both hoped to use the power of the state to find some solution to the economic aspects of the crisis.
text_raw:
Both  hoped  to
use  the  power  of  the  state  to  find  some  solution  to  the  economic  aspects  of  the  crisis.

text: This dualist struggle dwindled with the rise of economic and social pluralism after 1945.
text_raw:
This
dualist  struggle  dwindled  with  the  rise  of  economic  and  social  pluralism  after  1945.

text: A Depression Accompanies Transition to Various Stages
text_raw: A  Depression  Accompanies  Transition  to  Various  Stages

text: The second notable feature of this whole development is that the transition of each stage to the next was associated with a period of depression or low economic activity.
text_raw:
The  second  notable  feature  of  this  whole  development  is  that  the  transition  of  each
stage  to  the  next  was  associated  with  a  period  of  depression  or  low  economic  activity.

text: This was because each stage, after an earlier progressive phase, became later, in its final phase, an organization of vested interests more concerned with protecting its established modes of action than in continuing progressive changes by the application of resources to new, improved methods.
text_raw:
This  was  because  each  stage,  after  an  earlier  progressive  phase,  became  later,  in  its  final
phase,  an  organization  of  vested  interests  more  concerned  with  protecting  its  established
modes  of  action  than  in  continuing  progressive  changes  by  the  application  of  resources  to
new,  improved  methods.

text: This is inevitable in any social organization, but is peculiarly so in regard to capitalism.
text_raw:
This  is  inevitable  in  any  social  organization,  but  is  peculiarly  so
in  regard  to  capitalism.

text: The Primary Goal of Capitalism
text_raw: The  Primary  Goal  of  Capitalism

text: The third notable feature of the whole development is closely related to this special nature of capitalism.
text_raw:
The  third  notable  feature  of  the  whole  development  is  closely  related  to  this  special
nature  of  capitalism.

text: Capitalism provides very powerful motivations for economic activity because it associates economic motivations so closely with self-interest.
text_raw:
Capitalism  provides  very  powerful  motivations  for  economic
activity  because  it  associates  economic  motivations  so  closely  with  self-interest.

text: But this same feature, which is a source of strength in providing economic motivation through the pursuit of profits, is also a source of weakness owing to the fact that so self-centered a motivation contributes very readily to a loss of economic coordination.
text_raw:
But  this
same  feature,  which  is  a  source  of  strength  in  providing  economic  motivation  through  the
pursuit  of  profits,  is  also  a  source  of  weakness  owing  to  the  fact  that  so  self-centered  a
motivation  contributes  very  readily  to  a  loss  of  economic  coordination.

text: Each individual, just because he is so powerfully motivated by self-interest, easily loses sight of the role which his own activities play in the economic system as a whole, and tends to act as if his activities were the whole, with inevitable injury to that whole.
text_raw:
Each  individual,
just  because  he  is  so  powerfully  motivated  by  self-interest,  easily  loses  sight  of  the  role
which  his  own  activities  play  in  the  economic  system  as  a  whole,  and  tends  to  act  as  if  his
activities  were  the  whole,  with  inevitable  injury  to  that  whole.

text: We could indicate this by pointing out that capitalism, because it seeks profits as its primary goal, is never primarily seeking to achieve prosperity, high production, high consumption, political power, patriotic improvement, or moral uplift.
text_raw:
We  could  indicate  this  by
pointing  out  that  capitalism,  because  it  seeks  profits  as  its  primary  goal,  is  never  primarily
seeking  to  achieve  prosperity,  high  production,  high  consumption,  political  power,
patriotic  improvement,  or  moral  uplift.

text: Any of these may be achieved under capitalism, and any (or all) of them may he sacrificed and lost under capitalism, depending on this relationship to the primary goal of capitalist activity â€” the pursuit of profits.
text_raw:
Any  of  these  may  be  achieved  under  capitalism,
and  any  (or  all)  of  them  may  he  sacrificed  and  lost  under  capitalism,  depending  on  this
relationship  to  the  primary  goal  of  capitalist  activity â€” the  pursuit  of  profits.

text: During the nine-hundred-year history of capitalism, it has, at various times, contributed both to the achievement and to the destruction of these other social goals.
text_raw:
During  the
nine-hundred-year  history  of  capitalism,  it  has,  at  various  times,  contributed  both  to  the
achievement  and  to  the  destruction  of  these  other  social  goals.

text: Commercial Capitalism
text_raw: Commercial  Capitalism

text: The different stages of capitalism have sought to win profits by different kinds of economic activities.
text_raw:
The  different  stages  of  capitalism  have  sought  to  win  profits  by  different  kinds  of
economic  activities.

text: The original stage, which we call commercial capitalism, sought profits by moving goods from one place to another.
text_raw:
The  original  stage,  which  we  call  commercial  capitalism,  sought
profits  by  moving  goods  from  one  place  to  another.

text: In this effort, goods went from places where they were less valuable to places where they were more valuable, while money, doing the same thing, moved in the opposite direction.
text_raw:
In  this  effort,  goods  went  from  places
where  they  were  less  valuable  to  places  where  they  were  more  valuable,  while  money,
doing  the  same  thing,  moved  in  the  opposite  direction.

text: This valuation, which determined the movement both of goods and of money and which made them move in opposite directions, was measured by the relationship between these two things.
text_raw:
This  valuation,  which  determined
the  movement  both  of  goods  and  of  money  and  which  made  them  move  in  opposite
directions,  was  measured  by  the  relationship  between  these  two  things.

text: Thus the value of goods was expressed in money, and the value of money was expressed in goods.
text_raw:
Thus  the  value  of
goods  was  expressed  in  money,  and  the  value  of  money  was  expressed  in  goods.

text: Goods moved from low-price areas to high-price areas, and money moved from high-price areas to low-price areas, because goods were more valuable where prices were high and money was more valuable where prices were low.
text_raw:
Goods
moved  from  low-price  areas  to  high-price  areas,  and  money  moved  from  high-price  areas
to  low-price  areas,  because  goods  were  more  valuable  where  prices  were  high  and  money
was  more  valuable  where  prices  were  low.

text: Money and Goods Are Different
text_raw: Money  and  Goods  Are  Different

text: Thus, clearly, money and goods are not the same thing but are, on the contrary, exactly opposite things.
text_raw:
Thus,  clearly,  money  and  goods  are  not  the  same  thing  but  are,  on  the  contrary,
exactly  opposite  things.

text: Most confusion in economic thinking arises from failure to recognize this fact.
text_raw:
Most  confusion  in  economic  thinking  arises  from  failure  to
recognize  this  fact.

text: Goods are wealth which you have, while money is a claim on wealth which you do not have.
text_raw:
Goods  are  wealth  which  you  have,  while  money  is  a  claim  on  wealth
which  you  do  not  have.

text: Thus goods are an asset; money is a debt.
text_raw: Thus  goods  are  an  asset;  money  is  a  debt.

text: If goods are wealth; money is not wealth, or negative wealth, or even anti- wealth.
text_raw:
If  goods  are  wealth;
money  is  not  wealth,  or  negative  wealth,  or  even  anti- wealth.

text: They always behave in opposite ways, just as they usually move in opposite directions.
text_raw:
They  always  behave  in
opposite  ways,  just  as  they  usually  move  in  opposite  directions.

text: If the value of one goes up, the value of the other goes down, and in the same proportion.
text_raw:
If  the  value  of  one  goes
up,  the  value  of  the  other  goes  down,  and  in  the  same  proportion.

text: The value of goods, expressed in money, is called "prices," while the value of money, expressed in goods, is called "value."
text_raw:
The  value  of  goods,
expressed  in  money,  is  called  "prices,"  while  the  value  of  money,  expressed  in  goods,  is
called  "value."

text: The Rise of Commercial Capitalism
text_raw: The  Rise  of  Commercial  Capitalism

text: Commercial capitalism arose when merchants, carrying goods from one area to another, were able to sell these goods at their destination for a price which covered original cost, all costs of moving the goods, including the merchant's expenses, and a profit.
text_raw:
Commercial  capitalism  arose  when  merchants,  carrying  goods  from  one  area  to
another,  were  able  to  sell  these  goods  at  their  destination  for  a  price  which  covered
original  cost,  all  costs  of  moving  the  goods,  including  the  merchant's  expenses,  and  a
profit.

text: This development, which began as the movement of luxury goods, increased wealth because it led to specialization of activities both in crafts and in agriculture, which increased skills and output, and also brought into the market new commodities.
text_raw:
This  development,  which  began  as  the  movement  of  luxury  goods,  increased
wealth  because  it  led  to  specialization  of  activities  both  in  crafts  and  in  agriculture,  which
increased  skills  and  output,  and  also  brought  into  the  market  new  commodities.

text: The Development of Mercantilism
text_raw: The  Development  of  Mercantilism

text: Eventually, this stage of commercial capitalism became institutionalized into a restrictive system, sometimes called "mercantilism," in which merchants sought to gain profits, not from the movements of goods but from restricting the movements of goods.
text_raw:
Eventually,  this  stage  of  commercial  capitalism  became  institutionalized  into  a
restrictive  system,  sometimes  called  "mercantilism,"  in  which  merchants  sought  to  gain
profits,  not  from  the  movements  of  goods  but  from  restricting  the  movements  of  goods.

text: Thus the pursuit of profits, which had earlier led to increased prosperity by increasing trade and production, became a restriction on both trade and production, because profit became an end in itself rather than an accessory mechanism in the economic system as a whole.
text_raw:
Thus  the  pursuit  of  profits,  which  had  earlier  led  to  increased  prosperity  by  increasing
trade  and  production,  became  a  restriction  on  both  trade  and  production,  because  profit
became  an  end  in  itself  rather  than  an  accessory  mechanism  in  the  economic  system  as  a
whole.

text: The way in which commercial capitalism (an expanding economic organization) was transformed into mercantilism (a restrictive economic organization) twice in our past history is very revealing not only of the nature of economic systems, and of men themselves, but also of the nature of economic crisis and what can be done about it.
text_raw:
The  way  in  which  commercial  capitalism  (an  expanding  economic  organization)  was
transformed  into  mercantilism  (a  restrictive  economic  organization)  twice  in  our  past
history  is  very  revealing  not  only  of  the  nature  of  economic  systems,  and  of  men
themselves,  but  also  of  the  nature  of  economic  crisis  and  what  can  be  done  about  it.

text: Merchants Restrict Trade to Increase Profits
text_raw: Merchants  Restrict  Trade  to  Increase  Profits

text: Under commercial capitalism, merchants soon discovered that an increasing flow of goods from a low-price area to a high-price area tended to raise prices in the former and to lower prices in the latter.
text_raw:
Under  commercial  capitalism,  merchants  soon  discovered  that  an  increasing  flow  of
goods  from  a  low-price  area  to  a  high-price  area  tended  to  raise  prices  in  the  former  and
to  lower  prices  in  the  latter.

text: Every time a shipment of spices came into London, the price of spices there began to fall, while the arrival of buyers and ships in Malacca gave prices there an upward spurt.
text_raw:
Every  time  a  shipment  of  spices  came  into  London,  the  price
of  spices  there  began  to  fall,  while  the  arrival  of  buyers  and  ships  in  Malacca  gave  prices
there  an  upward  spurt.

text: This trend toward equalization of price levels between two areas because of the double, and reciprocal, movement of goods and money jeopardized profits for merchants, however much it may have satisfied producers and consumers at either end.
text_raw:
This  trend  toward  equalization  of  price  levels  between  two  areas
because  of  the  double,  and  reciprocal,  movement  of  goods  and  money  jeopardized  profits
for  merchants,  however  much  it  may  have  satisfied  producers  and  consumers  at  either
end.

text: It did this by reducing the price differential between the two areas and thus reducing the margin within which the merchant could make his profit.
text_raw:
It  did  this  by  reducing  the  price  differential  between  the  two  areas  and  thus  reducing
the  margin  within  which  the  merchant  could  make  his  profit.

text: It did not take shrewd merchants long to realize that they could maintain this price differential, and thus their profits, if they could restrict the flow of goods, so that an equal volume of money flowed for a reduced volume of goods.
text_raw:
It  did  not  take  shrewd
merchants  long  to  realize  that  they  could  maintain  this  price  differential,  and  thus  their
profits,  if  they  could  restrict  the  flow  of  goods,  so  that  an  equal  volume  of  money  flowed
for  a  reduced  volume  of  goods.

text: In this way, shipments were decreased, costs were reduced, but profits were maintained.
text_raw:
In  this  way,  shipments  were  decreased,  costs  were
reduced,  but  profits  were  maintained.

text: Two things are notable in this mercantilist situation.
text_raw: Two  things  are  notable  in  this  mercantilist  situation.

text: In the first place, the merchant, by his restrictive practices, was, in essence, increasing his own satisfaction by reducing that of the producer at one end and of the consumer at the other end; he was able to do this because he was in the middle between them.
text_raw:
In  the  first  place,  the  merchant,
by  his  restrictive  practices,  was,  in  essence,  increasing  his  own  satisfaction  by  reducing

text: Britain's Victory Over Napoleon
text_raw: Britain's  Victory  Over  Napoleon

text: Britain's victory over Napoleon was also helped by two economic innovations: the Agricultural Revolution, which was well established there in 1720, and the Industrial Revolution, which was equally well established there by 1776, when Watt patented his steam engine.
text_raw:
Britain's  victory  over  Napoleon  was  also  helped  by  two  economic  innovations:  the
Agricultural  Revolution,  which  was  well  established  there  in  1720,  and  the  Industrial
Revolution,  which  was  equally  well  established  there  by  1776,  when  Watt  patented  his
steam  engine.

text: The Industrial Revolution, like the Credit Revolution, has been much misunderstood, both at the time and since.
text_raw:
The  Industrial  Revolution,  like  the  Credit  Revolution,  has  been  much
misunderstood,  both  at  the  time  and  since.

text: This is unfortunate, as each of these has great significance, both to advanced and to underdeveloped countries, in the twentieth century.
text_raw:
This  is  unfortunate,  as  each  of  these  has  great
significance,  both  to  advanced  and  to  underdeveloped  countries,  in  the  twentieth  century.

text: The Industrial Revolution was accompanied by a number of incidental features, such as growth of cities through the factory system, the rapid growth of an unskilled labor supply (the proletariat), the reduction of labor to the status of a commodity in the competitive market, and the shifting of ownership of tools and equipment from laborers to a new social class of entrepreneurs.
text_raw:
The  Industrial  Revolution  was  accompanied  by  a  number  of  incidental  features,  such  as
growth  of  cities  through  the  factory  system,  the  rapid  growth  of  an  unskilled  labor  supply
(the  proletariat),  the  reduction  of  labor  to  the  status  of  a  commodity  in  the  competitive
market,  and  the  shifting  of  ownership  of  tools  and  equipment  from  laborers  to  a  new
social  class  of  entrepreneurs.

text: None of these constituted the essential feature of industrialism, which was, in fact, the application of nonliving power to the productive process.
text_raw:
None  of  these  constituted  the  essential  feature  of
industrialism,  which  was,  in  fact,  the  application  of  nonliving  power  to  the  productive
process.

text: This application, symbolized in the steam engine and the water wheel, in the long run served to reduce or eliminate the relative significance of unskilled labor and the use of human or animal energy in the productive process (automation) and to disperse the productive process from cities, but did so, throughout, by intensifying the vital feature of the system, the use of energy from sources other than living bodies.

text: The Rise of Large Industrial Enterprises in Britain
text_raw: The  Rise  of  Large  Industrial  Enterprises  in  Britain

text: In this continuing process, Britain's early achievement of industrialism gave it such great profits that these, combined with the profits derived earlier from commercial capitalism and the simultaneous profits derived from the unearned rise in land values from new cities and mines, made its early industrial enterprises largely self-financed or at least locally financed.
text_raw:
In  this  continuing  process,  Britain's  early  achievement  of  industrialism  gave  it  such
great  profits  that  these,  combined  with  the  profits  derived  earlier  from  commercial
capitalism  and  the  simultaneous  profits  derived  from  the  unearned  rise  in  land  values
from  new  cities  and  mines,  made  its  early  industrial  enterprises  largely  self-financed  or  at
least  locally  financed.

text: They were organized in proprietorships and partnerships, had contact with local deposit banks for short-term current loans, but had little to do with international bankers, investment banks, central governments, or corporative forms of business organization.
text_raw:
They  were  organized  in  proprietorships  and  partnerships,  had
contact  with  local  deposit  banks  for  short-term  current  loans,  but  had  little  to  do  with
international  bankers,  investment  banks,  central  governments,  or  corporative  forms  of
business  organization.

text: This early stage of industrial capitalism, which lasted in England from about 1770 to about 1850, was shared to some extent with Belgium and even France, but took quite different forms in the United States, Germany, and Italy, and almost totally different forms in Russia or Asia.
text_raw:
This  early  stage  of  industrial  capitalism,  which  lasted  in  England  from  about  1770  to
about  1850,  was  shared  to  some  extent  with  Belgium  and  even  France,  but  took  quite
different  forms  in  the  United  States,  Germany,  and  Italy,  and  almost  totally  different
forms  in  Russia  or  Asia.

text: The chief reason for these differences was the need for raising funds (capital) to pay for the rearrangement of the factors of production (]and, labor, materials, skill, equipment, and so on) which industrialism required.

materials,  skill,  equipment,  and  so  on)  which  industrialism  required.

text_raw: The  Role  of  the  International  Investment  Banker

text: The more difficulty an area had in mobilizing capital for industrialization, the more significant was the role of investment bankers and of governments in the industrial process.

significant  was  the  role  of  investment  bankers  and  of  governments  in  the  industrial

text: In fact, the early forms of industrialism based on textiles, iron, coal, and steam spread so slowly from England to Europe that England was itself entering upon the next stage, financial capitalism, by the time Germany and the United States (about 1850) were just beginning to industrialize.
text_raw:
In  fact,  the  early  forms  of  industrialism  based  on  textiles,  iron,  coal,  and  steam
spread  so  slowly  from  England  to  Europe  that  England  was  itself  entering  upon  the  next
stage,  financial  capitalism,  by  the  time  Germany  and  the  United  States  (about  1850)  were
just  beginning  to  industrialize.

text: This new stage of financial capitalism, which continued to dominate England, France, and the United States as late as 1930, was made necessary by the great mobilizations of capital needed for railroad building after 1830.
text_raw:
This  new  stage  of  financial  capitalism,  which  continued  to
dominate  England,  France,  and  the  United  States  as  late  as  1930,  was  made  necessary  by
the  great  mobilizations  of  capital  needed  for  railroad  building  after  1830.

text: Financial Capitalism, 1850 - 1931
text_raw: Financial  Capitalism,  1850  -  1931

text: This third stage of capitalism is of such overwhelming significance in the history of the twentieth century, and its ramifications and influences have been so subterranean and even occult, that we may be excused if we devote considerate attention to its organization and methods.
text_raw:
This  third  stage  of  capitalism  is  of  such  overwhelming  significance  in  the  history  of
the  twentieth  century,  and  its  ramifications  and  influences  have  been  so  subterranean  and
even  occult,  that  we  may  be  excused  if  we  devote  considerate  attention  to  its  organization
and  methods.

text: Essentially what it did was to take the old disorganized and localized methods of handling money and credit and organize them into an integrated system, on an international basis, which worked with incredible and well-oiled facility for many decades.
text_raw:
Essentially  what  it  did  was  to  take  the  old  disorganized  and  localized
methods  of  handling  money  and  credit  and  organize  them  into  an  integrated  system,  on
an  international  basis,  which  worked  with  incredible  and  well-oiled  facility  for  many
decades.

text: The center of that system was in London, with major offshoots in New York and Paris, and it has left, as its greatest achievement, an integrated banking system and a heavily capitalized â€” if now largely obsolescent â€” framework of heavy industry, reflected in railroads, steel mills, coal mines, and electrical utilities.

heavily  capitalized â€” if  now  largely  obsolescent â€” framework  of  heavy  industry,  reflected

text: This system had its center in London for four chief reasons.

text: Second was England's oligarchic social structure (especially as reflected in its concentrated landownership and limited access to educational opportunities) which provided a very inequitable distribution of incomes with large surpluses coming to the control of a small, energetic upper class.
