than  in  Mongolia,  Siberia,  or  even  northern  China,  persuaded  Japan  to  accept  the  change
of  direction.

text: A Soviet ambassador returned to Tokyo in November 1939, for the first time since June 1938.
text_raw:
A  Soviet  ambassador  returned  to  Tokyo  in  November  1939,  for  the  first  time
since  June  1938.

text: During the period 1929 to October 1941, the Soviet Union had excellent information about Japanese affairs from its "master spy" in the Far East, Richard Sorge.
text_raw:
During  the  period  1929  to  October  1941,  the  Soviet  Union  had  excellent  information
about  Japanese  affairs  from  its  "master  spy"  in  the  Far  East,  Richard  Sorge.

text: Sorge, a member of the Nazi Party from 1933, representative of many German newspapers in Tokyo from the same year, and press attache in the German Embassy in Tokyo in 1939- 1941, had an excellent knowledge of the most secret matters in the Far East because of his own intimate relations with the German ambassador and because of his secret agents (including Saionji, adopted son of the "last Genro," and Ozaki, adviser to Prince Konoye) in Japanese governing circles.
text_raw:
Sorge,  a
member  of  the  Nazi  Party  from  1933,  representative  of  many  German  newspapers  in
Tokyo  from  the  same  year,  and  press  attache  in  the  German  Embassy  in  Tokyo  in  1939-
1941,  had  an  excellent  knowledge  of  the  most  secret  matters  in  the  Far  East  because  of
his  own  intimate  relations  with  the  German  ambassador  and  because  of  his  secret  agents
(including  Saionji,  adopted  son  of  the  "last  Genro,"  and  Ozaki,  adviser  to  Prince  Konoye)
in  Japanese  governing  circles.

text: By reporting to Moscow on the condition of the Japanese military forces and the gradual triumph, within the Japanese government, of the anti- British over the anti-Russian influence, Sorge made it possible for the Soviet Union to weaken its defenses in the Far East in order to strengthen them in Europe.
text_raw:
By  reporting  to  Moscow  on  the  condition  of  the  Japanese
military  forces  and  the  gradual  triumph,  within  the  Japanese  government,  of  the  anti-
British  over  the  anti-Russian  influence,  Sorge  made  it  possible  for  the  Soviet  Union  to
weaken  its  defenses  in  the  Far  East  in  order  to  strengthen  them  in  Europe.

text: In Europe, after the occupation of Poland (which shielded the Russian center), the Soviet leaders were worried about two areas.
text_raw:
In  Europe,  after  the  occupation  of  Poland  (which  shielded  the  Russian  center),  the
Soviet  leaders  were  worried  about  two  areas.

text: In the south, including the Balkans, the Dardanelles, or the Caspian oil fields, they were very fearful of an Anglo-French attack, while in the Baltic they were fearful of both the Western Powers and Germany.
text_raw:
In  the  south,  including  the  Balkans,  the
Dardanelles,  or  the  Caspian  oil  fields,  they  were  very  fearful  of  an  Anglo-French  attack,
while  in  the  Baltic  they  were  fearful  of  both  the  Western  Powers  and  Germany.

text: The Soviet fears of the Western Powers in the south appear quite unfounded to us, but seemed very real to them in 1939.
text_raw:
The  Soviet  fears  of  the  Western  Powers  in  the  south  appear  quite  unfounded  to  us,  but
seemed  very  real  to  them  in  1939.

text: The information which has been released since 1945 shows that there was some basis for this fear but that the Anglo-French threat to Russia was much greater in the Baltic than it was in the south.
text_raw:
The  information  which  has  been  released  since  1945
shows  that  there  was  some  basis  for  this  fear  but  that  the  Anglo-French  threat  to  Russia
was  much  greater  in  the  Baltic  than  it  was  in  the  south.

text: In the latter area the Kremlin was suspicious of the French Army of the Orient in Syria.
text_raw:
In  the  latter  area  the  Kremlin  was
suspicious  of  the  French  Army  of  the  Orient  in  Syria.

text: The Russians believed that General Maxime Weygand had a force of several hundred thousand men which he wished to use across Iran or Turkey in an attack on the Russian oil fields in the Caspian region.
text_raw:
The  Russians  believed  that  General
Maxime  Weygand  had  a  force  of  several  hundred  thousand  men  which  he  wished  to  use
across  Iran  or  Turkey  in  an  attack  on  the  Russian  oil  fields  in  the  Caspian  region.

text: In January 1940, Germany obtained reports from Paris that Weygand proposed to attack the Soviet Union from Romania.
text_raw:
In
January  1940,  Germany  obtained  reports  from  Paris  that  Weygand  proposed  to  attack  the
Soviet  Union  from  Romania.

text: As a matter of fact, Wevgatld had only three poorly equipped divisions totaling about 40,000 men, and his plans were largely defensive.
text_raw:
As  a  matter  of  fact,  Wevgatld  had  only  three  poorly
equipped  divisions  totaling  about  40,000  men,  and  his  plans  were  largely  defensive.

text: He hoped to support the Allied guarantees to Turkey, Greece, and Romania (given in April 1939), and to protect the Romanian oil fields by moving northward from Salonika if Germany, Hungary, or Bulgaria made any warlike move in the Balkans.
text_raw:
He
hoped  to  support  the  Allied  guarantees  to  Turkey,  Greece,  and  Romania  (given  in  April
1939),  and  to  protect  the  Romanian  oil  fields  by  moving  northward  from  Salonika  if
Germany,  Hungary,  or  Bulgaria  made  any  warlike  move  in  the  Balkans.

text: The political situation in the Balkans was of such precarious stability that the Western Powers did not dare to make a move in the area for fear everything would collapse.
text_raw:
The  political  situation  in  the  Balkans  was  of  such  precarious  stability  that  the  Western
Powers  did  not  dare  to  make  a  move  in  the  area  for  fear  everything  would  collapse.

text: Turkey, Greece, Romania, and Yugoslavia were joined in a Balkan Entente aimed at preventing any Bulgarian aggression.
text_raw:
Turkey,  Greece,  Romania,  and  Yugoslavia  were  joined  in  a  Balkan  Entente  aimed  at
preventing  any  Bulgarian  aggression.

text: Since these four states could mobilize over a hundred divisions, although lacking all modern or heavy equipment, they could keep Bulgaria quiet.
text_raw:
Since  these  four  states  could  mobilize  over  a
hundred  divisions,  although  lacking  all  modern  or  heavy  equipment,  they  could  keep
Bulgaria  quiet.

text: Unfortunately, the Balkan Entente was not designed for protection against Italy or Germany, where the real danger lay.
text_raw:
Unfortunately,  the  Balkan  Entente  was  not  designed  for  protection  against
Italy  or  Germany,  where  the  real  danger  lay.

text: Italy had various projects to attack Greece from the Albanian territory it had seized in April 1939.
text_raw:
Italy  had  various  projects  to  attack  Greece  from  the  Albanian  territory  it  had  seized  in
April  1939.

text: It also had fully matured plans to disrupt Yugoslavia by subsidizing and supporting a Croat revolt, under Ante Paveliae, against the dominant Serb majority in that
text_raw:
It  also  had  fully  matured  plans  to  disrupt  Yugoslavia  by  subsidizing  and
supporting  a  Croat  revolt,  under  Ante  Paveliae,  against  the  dominant  Serb  majority  in  that

text: state.
text_raw: state.

text: During the "phony war" the Italians hoped that the Western Powers would allow Italy to carry out its project against Yugoslavia in order to block any German movement into that area.
text_raw:
During  the  "phony  war"  the  Italians  hoped  that  the  Western  Powers  would  allow
Italy  to  carry  out  its  project  against  Yugoslavia  in  order  to  block  any  German  movement
into  that  area.

text: Such permission seemed possible from the fact that the democratic states had not guaranteed Yugoslavia as they had the other three states of the Balkan Entente.
text_raw:
Such  permission  seemed  possible  from  the  fact  that  the  democratic  states
had  not  guaranteed  Yugoslavia  as  they  had  the  other  three  states  of  the  Balkan  Entente.

text: Italy's project Noms set for early June 1940, but was interrupted by Hitler's attack in the West, which was made, without notifying his Italian partner, on May 10th.
text_raw:
Italy's  project  Noms  set  for  early  June  1940,  but  was  interrupted  by  Hitler's  attack  in  the
West,  which  was  made,  without  notifying  his  Italian  partner,  on  May  10th.

text: Another element of instability in southeastern Europe was the position of Hungary, which aspired to detach Transylvania from Romania.
text_raw:
Another  element  of  instability  in  southeastern  Europe  was  the  position  of  Hungary,
which  aspired  to  detach  Transylvania  from  Romania.

text: Since Hungary could not take this area by its own power, it sought support from Italy rather than from Germany (which the Hungarians feared).
text_raw:
Since  Hungary  could  not  take  this
area  by  its  own  power,  it  sought  support  from  Italy  rather  than  from  Germany  (which  the
Hungarians  feared).

text: With Italian support, Hungary refused to allow German troops to cross its territory to attack Poland in September 1939, and began to negotiate an agreement with Italy by which the Duke of Aosta would be offered the crown of Hungary, as an anti-German solution to Hungary's ambiguous constitutional position.
text_raw:
With  Italian  support,  Hungary  refused  to  allow  German  troops  to
cross  its  territory  to  attack  Poland  in  September  1939,  and  began  to  negotiate  an
agreement  with  Italy  by  which  the  Duke  of  Aosta  would  be  offered  the  crown  of
Hungary,  as  an  anti-German  solution  to  Hungary's  ambiguous  constitutional  position.

text: This project, like the one in Croatia, was upset by the growing rivalry of Germany and Russia in the Balkans.
text_raw:
This  project,  like  the  one  in  Croatia,  was  upset  by  the  growing  rivalry  of  Germany  and
Russia  in  the  Balkans.

text: During the period from September 1939 to June 1940, Hitler had no political ambitions with respect to the Balkans or the Soviet Union.
text_raw:
During  the  period  from  September  1939  to  June  1940,  Hitler  had  no  political
ambitions  with  respect  to  the  Balkans  or  the  Soviet  Union.

text: From both he wanted nothing more than the maximum supply of raw materials and a political peace which would permit these goods to flow to Germany.
text_raw:
From  both  he  wanted  nothing
more  than  the  maximum  supply  of  raw  materials  and  a  political  peace  which  would
permit  these  goods  to  flow  to  Germany.

text: Both areas cooperated fully with Germany in economic matters, but fear of Germany was so great that both areas also sought political changes which might strengthen their ability to resist Germany at a later date.
text_raw:
Both  areas  cooperated  fully  with  Germany  in
economic  matters,  but  fear  of  Germany  was  so  great  that  both  areas  also  sought  political
changes  which  might  strengthen  their  ability  to  resist  Germany  at  a  later  date.

text: Hungarian efforts to obtain support from Italy were not successful, as we have seen, because Italy wavered between fear of Germany and recognition of the fact that its own ambitions in the Balkans, the Mediterranean, or Africa could be obtained only with German support.
text_raw:
Hungarian
efforts  to  obtain  support  from  Italy  were  not  successful,  as  we  have  seen,  because  Italy
wavered  between  fear  of  Germany  and  recognition  of  the  fact  that  its  own  ambitions  in
the  Balkans,  the  Mediterranean,  or  Africa  could  be  obtained  only  with  German  support.

text: The Balkan Entente sought support and military supplies from the Western Powers but could obtain little, since these Powers believed that they did not have the equipment to defend themselves.
text_raw:
The  Balkan  Entente  sought  support  and  military  supplies  from  the  Western  Powers  but
could  obtain  little,  since  these  Powers  believed  that  they  did  not  have  the  equipment  to
defend  themselves.

text: The only important step they took was a military alliance with Turkey.
text_raw:
The  only  important  step  they  took  was  a  military  alliance  with
Turkey.

text: This was signed with France and England on October 19, 1939 in the form of a mutual-assistance pact, except that Turkey could not be compelled to take up arms against Russia.
text_raw:
This  was  signed  with  France  and  England  on  October  19,  1939  in  the  form  of  a
mutual-assistance  pact,  except  that  Turkey  could  not  be  compelled  to  take  up  arms
against  Russia.

text: This last clause was inserted on Turkish insistence but was kept secret and, in consequence, the Soviet Union was not reassured by the agreement.
text_raw:
This  last  clause  was  inserted  on  Turkish  insistence  but  was  kept  secret
and,  in  consequence,  the  Soviet  Union  was  not  reassured  by  the  agreement.

text: In the meantime the Soviet Union took steps to defend itself against any attack from the Baltic.
text_raw:
In  the  meantime  the  Soviet  Union  took  steps  to  defend  itself  against  any  attack  from
the  Baltic.

text: In the period September 29-October 10, 1939, three of the Baltic states, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, were forced to sign military-assistance pacts with Russia.
text_raw:
In  the  period  September  29-October  10,  1939,  three  of  the  Baltic  states,
Estonia,  Latvia,  and  Lithuania,  were  forced  to  sign  military-assistance  pacts  with  Russia.

text: Estonia and Latvia provided naval and air bases for Russian forces, while the City of Vilna was given to Lithuania by Russia.
text_raw:
Estonia  and  Latvia  provided  naval  and  air  bases  for  Russian  forces,  while  the  City  of
Vilna  was  given  to  Lithuania  by  Russia.

text: About 25,000 Russian troops were stationed in each of the three countries.
text_raw:
About  25,000  Russian  troops  were  stationed  in
each  of  the  three  countries.

text: Appeals from these countries to Germany for support against Russia were summarily rejected, and they were advised to yield to the Soviet demands.
text_raw:
Appeals  from  these  countries  to  Germany  for  support  against
Russia  were  summarily  rejected,  and  they  were  advised  to  yield  to  the  Soviet  demands.

text: As part of the reorganization of this area, Hitler on September 27th ordered that the so- called "Baits" (German- speaking residents of the Baltic states) should be moved to Germany as quickly as possible.
text_raw:
As  part  of  the  reorganization  of  this  area,  Hitler  on  September  27th  ordered  that  the  so-
called  "Baits"  (German- speaking  residents  of  the  Baltic  states)  should  be  moved  to
Germany  as  quickly  as  possible.

text: This was done within a month.
text_raw: This  was  done  within  a  month.

text: From the Soviet point of view Finland provided a much more important problem than any of the Baltic states.
text_raw:
From  the  Soviet  point  of  view  Finland  provided  a  much  more  important  problem  than
any  of  the  Baltic  states.

text: The city of Leningrad, one of Russia's greatest industrial centers with a population of 3,191,000 persons, was joined to the Baltic Sea by the Gulf of Finland.
text_raw:
The  city  of  Leningrad,  one  of  Russia's  greatest  industrial  centers
with  a  population  of  3,191,000  persons,  was  joined  to  the  Baltic  Sea  by  the  Gulf  of
Finland.

text: This gulf, about 150 miles long and so miles wide, ran west to east, with its northern and eastern shores occupied by Finland and its southern shore largely Estonian.
text_raw:
This  gulf,  about  150  miles  long  and  so  miles  wide,  ran  west  to  east,  with  its
northern  and  eastern  shores  occupied  by  Finland  and  its  southern  shore  largely  Estonian.

text: Leningrad, at the extreme southeastern corner of the gulf, was at the southern end of the Karelian Isthmus, a neck of land running north and south between the gulf and Lake Ladoga, some 20 miles farther east.
text_raw:
Leningrad,  at  the  extreme  southeastern  corner  of  the  gulf,  was  at  the  southern  end  of  the
Karelian  Isthmus,  a  neck  of  land  running  north  and  south  between  the  gulf  and  Lake
Ladoga,  some  20  miles  farther  east.

text: The Finnish frontier crossed this isthmus from the gulf to Lake Ladoga only 20 miles north of Leningrad.
text_raw:
The  Finnish  frontier  crossed  this  isthmus  from  the
gulf  to  Lake  Ladoga  only  20  miles  north  of  Leningrad.

text: On October 14th the Soviet Union demanded that the Finnish frontier north of Leningrad be pushed back along the shore of the gulf so that the frontier would run westward from Lake Ladoga instead of southward as formerly.
text_raw:
On  October  14th  the  Soviet  Union  demanded  that  the  Finnish  frontier  north  of
Leningrad  be  pushed  back  along  the  shore  of  the  gulf  so  that  the  frontier  would  run
westward  from  Lake  Ladoga  instead  of  southward  as  formerly.

text: This would put the Finnish frontier about 50 miles from Leningrad, leaving Finland about half of the Karelian Isthmus.
text_raw:
This  would  put  the
Finnish  frontier  about  50  miles  from  Leningrad,  leaving  Finland  about  half  of  the
Karelian  Isthmus.

text: In addition, the Bolsheviks demanded a 30-year lease on the Finnish naval base at Hango at the entrance to the Gulf of Finland, a strip about 100 miles long and 10 miles wide in central Finland (where the Finnish frontier came closest to the railroad line between Leningrad and Russia's ice-free port of Murmansk on the Arctic Sea), and a small area of about 25 square miles where the Finnish frontier reached the Arctic Ocean west of Murmansk.
text_raw:
In  addition,  the  Bolsheviks  demanded  a  30-year  lease  on  the  Finnish
naval  base  at  Hango  at  the  entrance  to  the  Gulf  of  Finland,  a  strip  about  100  miles  long
and  10  miles  wide  in  central  Finland  (where  the  Finnish  frontier  came  closest  to  the
railroad  line  between  Leningrad  and  Russia's  ice-free  port  of  Murmansk  on  the  Arctic
Sea),  and  a  small  area  of  about  25  square  miles  where  the  Finnish  frontier  reached  the
Arctic  Ocean  west  of  Murmansk.

text: In return for these concessions Moscow offered a nonaggression pact, about 2,100 square miles of wooded area in central Finland, and permission to Finland to fortify the Aaland Islands between Finland and Sweden, something which had been forbidden since 1921.
text_raw:
In  return  for  these  concessions  Moscow  offered  a
nonaggression  pact,  about  2,100  square  miles  of  wooded  area  in  central  Finland,  and
permission  to  Finland  to  fortify  the  Aaland  Islands  between  Finland  and  Sweden,
something  which  had  been  forbidden  since  1921.

text: It is not yet clear why Finland rejected the Russian demands of October 1939.
text_raw: It  is  not  yet  clear  why  Finland  rejected  the  Russian  demands  of  October  1939.

text: The Germans and Russians believed that it was done under British influence, but the evidence is not available.
text_raw:
The
Germans  and  Russians  believed  that  it  was  done  under  British  influence,  but  the  evidence
is  not  available.

text: At any rate, the Finn asked for German support and were rebuffed as early as October 6-7 1939 (before the Russian demands were received); they ordered mobilization of their armed forces against the Soviet Union on October 8th, and were reported by the German minister to be "completely mobilized" ten days later.
text_raw:
At  any  rate,  the  Finn  asked  for  German  support  and  were  rebuffed  as
early  as  October  6-7  1939  (before  the  Russian  demands  were  received);  they  ordered
mobilization  of  their  armed  forces  against  the  Soviet  Union  on  October  8th,  and  were
reported  by  the  German  minister  to  be  "completely  mobilized"  ten  days  later.

text: In the negotiations Stalin abandoned the Soviet demand for Hango if he could get the Island of Russaro nearby and the island of Suursaari farther up the gulf, but insisted on most of the Karelian demand; the Finns offered about a third of the Karelian demand but refused to grant any naval bases in the gulf.
text_raw:
In  the
negotiations  Stalin  abandoned  the  Soviet  demand  for  Hango  if  he  could  get  the  Island  of
Russaro  nearby  and  the  island  of  Suursaari  farther  up  the  gulf,  but  insisted  on  most  of  the
Karelian  demand;  the  Finns  offered  about  a  third  of  the  Karelian  demand  but  refused  to
grant  any  naval  bases  in  the  gulf.

text: On November 8th the discussions broke down; four days later the Finnish negotiators went home.
text_raw:
On  November  8th  the  discussions  broke  down;  four
days  later  the  Finnish  negotiators  went  home.

text: For some unexplained reason, the Finns seem to have felt that the Russians would not attack their country, but the Soviets attacked at several points on November 28th.
text_raw:
For  some  unexplained  reason,  the  Finns
seem  to  have  felt  that  the  Russians  would  not  attack  their  country,  but  the  Soviets
attacked  at  several  points  on  November  28th.

text: If the Finns had misinterpreted the Soviet determination to attack, the Soviets misinterpreted the Finnish determination to resist.
text_raw:
If  the  Finns  had  misinterpreted  the  Soviet  determination  to  attack,  the  Soviets
misinterpreted  the  Finnish  determination  to  resist.

text: Although attacked at five major points by large forces with heavy equipment, the Finns made very skillful use of the terrain and the winter weather.
text_raw:
Although  attacked  at  five  major  points
by  large  forces  with  heavy  equipment,  the  Finns  made  very  skillful  use  of  the  terrain  and
the  winter  weather.

text: In the first two months (December-January) a half-dozen or more Soviet divisions were torn to pieces.
text_raw:
In  the  first  two  months  (December-January)  a  half-dozen  or  more
Soviet  divisions  were  torn  to  pieces.

text: Only in February 1940 did the Soviet offensive begin to move, and by the end of the month Finland's forces were so exhausted by superior numbers that they accepted the Soviet terms.
text_raw:
Only  in  February  1940  did  the  Soviet  offensive
begin  to  move,  and  by  the  end  of  the  month  Finland's  forces  were  so  exhausted  by
superior  numbers  that  they  accepted  the  Soviet  terms.

text: Peace was signed on March 12, 1940.
text_raw:
Peace  was  signed  on  March  12,
1940.

text: As soon as Finland realized that Russia seriously intended to attack, it set up a new Cabinet under Risto Ryti to wage the war and simultaneously seek peace by negotiation.
text_raw:
As  soon  as  Finland  realized  that  Russia  seriously  intended  to  attack,  it  set  up  a  new
Cabinet  under  Risto  Ryti  to  wage  the  war  and  simultaneously  seek  peace  by  negotiation.

text: This latter proved to be difficult because on December 2nd, Moscow set up a puppet Finnish government under a minor and discredited Finnish Communist in exile, V.
text_raw:
This  latter  proved  to  be  difficult  because  on  December  2nd,  Moscow  set  up  a  puppet
Finnish  government  under  a  minor  and  discredited  Finnish  Communist  in  exile,  V.

text: Kuusinen; a mutual-aid pact was signed with this puppet state at once.
text_raw: Kuusinen;  a  mutual-aid  pact  was  signed  with  this  puppet  state  at  once.

text: The existence of this regime discouraged Germany from offering any mediation seeking peace, in spite of its eagerness to see the end of the fighting in Finland, but on March 12th, when peace was made with the authentic Finnish government, Kuusinen was simply left in the lurch by Moscow.
text_raw:
The  existence  of
this  regime  discouraged  Germany  from  offering  any  mediation  seeking  peace,  in  spite  of
its  eagerness  to  see  the  end  of  the  fighting  in  Finland,  but  on  March  12th,  when  peace

text: The Soviet attack on Finland provided the leaders in the Entente countries with a heaven-sent opportunity to change the declared but un-fought war with Germany, which they did not want, into an undeclared but fighting war against the Soviet Union.
text_raw:
The  Soviet  attack  on  Finland  provided  the  leaders  in  the  Entente  countries  with  a
heaven-sent  opportunity  to  change  the  declared  but  un-fought  war  with  Germany,  which
they  did  not  want,  into  an  undeclared  but  fighting  war  against  the  Soviet  Union.

text: The fact that a Russian war would be hundreds of miles away, while the war with Germany was on their doorstep, was an added advantage, especially in Paris, which had been steadily resisting British suggestions for any unfriendly action against Germany along the Rhine.
text_raw:
The  fact
that  a  Russian  war  would  be  hundreds  of  miles  away,  while  the  war  with  Germany  was

resisting  British  suggestions  for  any  unfriendly  action  against  Germany  along  the  Rhine.

text: Accordingly, Britain and France resurrected the moribund League of Nations, violated the Covenant to put Finland, Egypt, and South Africa on the Council, and illegally (according to the American Journal of International Law) expelled Russia from the League as an aggressor.

(according  to  the  American  Journal  of  International  Law)  expelled  Russia  from  the
League  as  an  aggressor.

text: That Russia was an unprovoked aggressor is beyond question, but there was at least a surface inconsistency between the violence of the Anglo-French reaction against Russian aggression in 1939 and the complacency with which they had viewed other aggressions in 1931-1939.

That  Russia  was  an  unprovoked  aggressor  is  beyond  question,  but  there  was  at  least  a

text: This last act of the League of Nations was its most efficient.

The  German  aggressions  of  1936-1939  had  not  even  been  submitted  to  the  League  of

divergent  British  and  American  ideas  on  aerial  bombardment  were  reconciled  in  what

destroying  civilian  morale  and  exhausting  German  manpower  as  well  as  destroying

text: Some of these changes are obvious: a shift from a period of democracy to an age of experts; from a world dominated by Europe, and even by Britain, to a world divided into three great blocs; from a world in which man still lived ... surrounded by nature, to a situation where nature is dominated, transformed and, in a sense, totally destroyed by man; from a system where man's greatest problems were the material ones of man's helplessness in the face of the natural threats of disease, starvation, and the unpredictability of natural catastrophes to the totally different system of the 1960's and 1970's where the greatest threat to man is man himself, and where his greatest problems are the social (and nonmaterial) ones of what his true goals of existence are and what use he should make of his immense power over the universe, including his fellow-men.

text: The growth of international law in the late medieval and Renaissance periods not only sought to make the distinctions we have indicated, as a reaction against "feudal disorder"; it also sought to make a sharp distinction between public and private authority (in order to get rid of the feudal doctrine of dominia) and to set up sharp criteria of public authority involving the new doctrine of sovereignty.
text_raw:
The  growth  of  international  law  in  the  late  medieval  and  Renaissance
periods  not  only  sought  to  make  the  distinctions  we  have  indicated,  as  a  reaction  against
"feudal  disorder";  it  also  sought  to  make  a  sharp  distinction  between  public  and  private
authority  (in  order  to  get  rid  of  the  feudal  doctrine  of  dominia)  and  to  set  up  sharp  criteria
of  public  authority  involving  the  new  doctrine  of  sovereignty.

text: One of the chief criteria of such sovereignty w-as ability to maintain the peace and to enforce both law and order over a definite territory; one of its greatest achievements was the elimination of arbitrary non- sovereign private powers such as robber barons on land or piracy on the sea.
text_raw:
One  of  the  chief  criteria  of
such  sovereignty  w-as  ability  to  maintain  the  peace  and  to  enforce  both  law  and  order
over  a  definite  territory;  one  of  its  greatest  achievements  was  the  elimination  of  arbitrary
non- sovereign  private  powers  such  as  robber  barons  on  land  or  piracy  on  the  sea.

text: Under this conception, ability to maintain la\v and order became the chief evidence of sovereignty, and the possession of sovereignty became the sole mark of public authority and the existence of a state.

text: But the achievement of nuclear weapons, by creating two super-Powers in a Cold War, destroyed the fact of the equality of states.

two  super-Powers  in  a  Cold  War,  destroyed  the  fact  of  the  equality  of  states.

text: This had the obvious result of creating Powers on two levels: ordinary and super; but it had the less obvious, and more significant, consequence of permitting the existence of states of lower levels of power, far below the level of ordinary Powers.

obvious  result  of  creating  Powers  on  two  levels:  ordinary  and  super;  but  it  had  the  less
obvious,  and  more  significant,  consequence  of  permitting  the  existence  of  states  of  lower
levels  of  power,  far  below  the  level  of  ordinary  Powers.

text: This arose because the nuclear stalemate of the two super-Powers created an umbrella of fear of precipitating nuclear war which falsified their abilities to act at all.

President  Eisenhower's  Security  Order  10450  of  April,  1  953.

text: The first change was that public employment no longer was a right but became a privilege; the second was that disloyalty was no longer the chief criterion, but security was; and the third change was that the government no longer had to prove anything derogatory, hut merely needed to have a doubt that a person's employment was consistent with the security of the country.
text_raw:
The  first  change  was  that
public  employment  no  longer  was  a  right  but  became  a  privilege;  the  second  was  that
disloyalty  was  no  longer  the  chief  criterion,  but  security  was;  and  the  third  change  was
that  the  government  no  longer  had  to  prove  anything  derogatory,  hut  merely  needed  to
have  a  doubt  that  a  person's  employment  was  consistent  with  the  security  of  the  country.

text: Taken together, these three modifications placed the burden of proof on the employee rather than on the accuser and made the area of proof so wide that it could hardly be met.

text: The motivations of the Eisenhower Administration were emotional and complex, and represent a sharp reaction against the forces of rationalization and science which we have discussed.
text_raw:
The  motivations  of  the  Eisenhower  Administration  were  emotional  and  complex,  and
represent  a  sharp  reaction  against  the  forces  of  rationalization  and  science  which  we  have
discussed.

text: They seem to have been based on three narrowing circles of outlook.
text_raw: They  seem  to  have  been  based  on  three  narrowing  circles  of  outlook.

text: Broadest of all was a violent neurotic rebellion of harassed middle-class persons against a longtime challenge to middle-class values arising from depression, war, insecurity, science, foreigners, and minority groups of all kinds.
text_raw:
Broadest
of  all  was  a  violent  neurotic  rebellion  of  harassed  middle-class  persons  against  a  longtime
challenge  to  middle-class  values  arising  from  depression,  war,  insecurity,  science,
foreigners,  and  minority  groups  of  all  kinds.

text: This broad problem will be discussed elsewhere.
text_raw:
This  broad  problem  will  be  discussed
elsewhere.

text: A second, and narrower, circle of outlook was the basic Republican opposition to all kinds of collective action, including collective security, social welfare, and national security.
text_raw:
A  second,  and  narrower,  circle  of  outlook  was  the  basic  Republican
opposition  to  all  kinds  of  collective  action,  including  collective  security,  social  welfare,

text: The third was the obsession of business wealth in the country with the wickedness of unbalanced budgets and high taxes.

the  wickedness  of  unbalanced  budgets  and  high  taxes.

text: The Republican opposition to collective action was, of course, of long standing.
text_raw: The  Republican  opposition  to  collective  action  was,  of  course,  of  long  standing.

text: It is not generally recognized that it appears frequently as an opposition to national security expenditures, especially to defense expenditures for men rather than for equipment, but often for both.

text: Such opposition by Republicans was generally true in the whole period following 1945, and is clearly shown in their votes in Congress.

Such  opposition  by  Republicans  was  generally  true  in  the  whole  period

these  records  it  is  clear  that  public  opinion  always  supported  large  defense  forces  and  did
not  object  to  higher  taxes  or  government  spending  to  sustain  them.

support  was  stronger  from  persons  of  lower  educational  and  income  levels,  although
generally  found  on  all  levels.

text: In sharp contrast to this, public opinion gave much less support to foreign aid, and such support was less on low-er educational or income levels and was reflected in far greater opposition to taxation or government spending for economic foreign aid than for defense forces.

In  sharp  contrast  to  this,  public  opinion  gave  much  less
support  to  foreign  aid,  and  such  support  was  less  on  low-er  educational  or  income  levels

text: Professor Huntington has illuminated this difference by an analysis of congressional voting records over the period 1945-1960.
text_raw:
Professor  Huntington  has  illuminated  this  difference  by  an  analysis  of  congressional
voting  records  over  the  period  1945-1960.

text: He has examined votes on 79 controversial defense issues in Congress over the 15-year period and found that a majority of Democrats voted pro-defense on 74 of the 79 issues, while a majority of Republicans voted pro-defense on only 39 of the 79 issues.
text_raw:
He  has  examined  votes  on  79  controversial
defense  issues  in  Congress  over  the  15-year  period  and  found  that  a  majority  of
Democrats  voted  pro-defense  on  74  of  the  79  issues,  while  a  majority  of  Republicans
voted  pro-defense  on  only  39  of  the  79  issues.

text: On all these issues, Democratic senators voted 78.8 percent pro-defense and Republican senators voted only 43 percent pro- defense, while Democratic representatives voted 78.4 percent pro-defense and Republican representatives voted 53.8 percent pro-defense.
text_raw:
On  all  these  issues,  Democratic  senators
voted  78.8  percent  pro-defense  and  Republican  senators  voted  only  43  percent  pro-
defense,  while  Democratic  representatives  voted  78.4  percent  pro-defense  and
Republican  representatives  voted  53.8  percent  pro-defense.

text: Moreover, the Republican votes in both Houses were less pro-defense in the Eisenhower period than in the Truman period, the Senate Republican pro-defense votes falling from 47.1 to 33 percent with the change in Administration, and the House Republican pro-defense votes falling from 54.8 to 50.4 percent.
text_raw:
Moreover,  the  Republican
votes  in  both  Houses  were  less  pro-defense  in  the  Eisenhower  period  than  in  the  Truman
period,  the  Senate  Republican  pro-defense  votes  falling  from  47.1  to  33  percent  with  the
change  in  Administration,  and  the  House  Republican  pro-defense  votes  falling  from  54.8
to  50.4  percent.

text: Moreover, analysis of these votes, on a sectional basis, shows that the Republican pro-defense votes were concentrated in the Northeast and on the Pacific Coast, while the Democratic pro-defense votes were spaced relatively evenly around the country.
text_raw:
Moreover,  analysis  of  these  votes,  on  a  sectional  basis,  shows  that  the
Republican  pro-defense  votes  were  concentrated  in  the  Northeast  and  on  the  Pacific
Coast,  while  the  Democratic  pro-defense  votes  were  spaced  relatively  evenly  around  the
country.

text: When we shift from the Congress to the Administration, we see that the Democratic Administration, while still pro-defense, was less so than Democratic congressmen, but that the Republican Administration, while not pro-defense, was somewhat more favorable to defense than Republican congressmen.
text_raw:
When  we  shift  from  the  Congress  to  the  Administration,  we  see  that  the  Democratic
Administration,  while  still  pro-defense,  was  less  so  than  Democratic  congressmen,  but
that  the  Republican  Administration,  while  not  pro-defense,  was  somewhat  more  favorable
to  defense  than  Republican  congressmen.

text: This situation can be explained in terms of three forces acting upon politicians:
text_raw: This  situation  can  be  explained  in  terms  of  three  forces  acting  upon  politicians:

text: (1) the need for votes, (2) the need for campaign contributions, and (3) awareness of world conditions.
text_raw:
(1)  the
need  for  votes,  (2)  the  need  for  campaign  contributions,  and  (3)  awareness  of  world

text: On the Democratic side, public opinion, which means votes, works from the people to congressmen, while awareness of world conditions works from outside upon the Administration and through it to Congress.

On  the  Democratic  side,  public  opinion,  which  means  votes,  works  from  the
people  to  congressmen,  while  awareness  of  world  conditions  works  from  outside  upon

The  lobbying  of  special-interest  groups

text_raw:
On  the  Republican  side  the  influence  of  special  interests  is  much  greater  simply
because  the  Republican  Party  is  the  party  of  middle-class  and  business  interests.

text: In fact, the influence of lobbying by special interests is so great that it makes both the Republican Congress and the Republican Administration relatively immune to the need for defense, with the immunity less general in the Administration than in the Congress because the former is compelled, by its position, to pay some attention to world conditions.
text_raw:
In  fact,
the  influence  of  lobbying  by  special  interests  is  so  great  that  it  makes  both  the  Republican
Congress  and  the  Republican  Administration  relatively  immune  to  the  need  for  defense,

former  is  compelled,  by  its  position,  to  pay  some  attention  to  world  conditions.

text: The Republican congressmen, on the other hand, are relatively immune both to public opinion and the pressure of world conditions, being shielded from the former by the influence of special-interest lobbyists and shielded from the latter by the Administration.

The
Republican  congressmen,  on  the  other  hand,  are  relatively  immune  both  to  public  opinion

text: In November 1954, three years before "Sputnik," a journalist asked Wilson for comment on the possibility that the Russians might beat the United States in the satellite race; the secretary replied, "I wouldn't care if they did." The culmination of all this was Wilson's orders of November and December 1956, which crippled the army's ability to use contemporary tactics by restricting it to missiles of less than 200 miles' range, and forbidding it to use planes of over five thousand pounds or helicopters of over ten thousand pounds' weight.

next  five  years,  in  a  struggle  for  power  whose  details  are  still  concealed,  Khrushchev  rose

text: The process by which he succeeded Stalin was almost a repetition of that by which Stalin had succeeded Lenin.
text_raw:
The  process  by  which  he  succeeded  Stalin  was  almost  a
repetition  of  that  by  which  Stalin  had  succeeded  Lenin.

text: In each case, the ultimately successful contender was the least prominent of a group of contenders; in each case this victor used the post of secretary of the party as the chief weapon in his upward rise; in each case, this rise was achieved by a series of chess moves in which the most powerful rival contenders were eliminated, one by one, in a series of shifts, beginning with the most dangerous (in one case Trotsky, in the later case Beria).
text_raw:
In  each  case,  the  ultimately
successful  contender  was  the  least  prominent  of  a  group  of  contenders;  in  each  case  this

each  case,  this  rise  was  achieved  by  a  series  of  chess  moves  in  which  the  most  powerful

most  dangerous  (in  one  case  Trotsky,  in  the  later  case  Beria).

Molotov  continued  to  insist  on  the  "hard"  policies  associated  with  Stalin,  full

workers  rose  up  against  the  Communist  government  in  East  Berlin.

briefcase,  found  his  pistol  gone,  and  looked  up  into  the  muzzle  of  his  own  gun.

text_raw:
But  the  mystery

text: One factor in the making of the speech was undoubtedly the determination of the army to clear itself of the unjust accusations made against its officers in 1937-1941 and against the effort to attribute the disasters of 1941-1942 to professional incompetence.
text_raw:

text: Just as the German generals after 1945 wanted to blame their defeats on Hitler, so the Russian generals, with much greater justification, wanted to blame their early defeats on Stalin.
text_raw:
Just  as  the  German  generals  after  1945  wanted  to  blame  their  defeats  on
Hitler,  so  the  Russian  generals,  with  much  greater  justification,  wanted  to  blame  their

text: But there undoubtedly must have been other causes of which we are not yet aware.

But  there  undoubtedly  must  have  been  other  causes  of  which  we

text: The anti-Stalin speech, like the admission of error in the alienation from Tito, inevitably had an injurious influence on Communism throughout the world, especially in the satellite Powers, and ultimately became the ideological basis for the splitting of these Powers into Stalinist and anti-Stalinist groupings led by Red China and the Soviet Union.
text_raw:
The  anti-Stalin  speech,  like  the  admission  of  error  in  the  alienation
from  Tito,  inevitably  had  an  injurious  influence  on  Communism  throughout  the  world,
especially  in  the  satellite  Powers,  and  ultimately  became  the  ideological  basis  for  the
splitting  of  these  Powers  into  Stalinist  and  anti-Stalinist  groupings  led  by  Red  China  and
the  Soviet  Union.

text: Certain points about this speech are noteworthy.
text_raw: Certain  points  about  this  speech  are  noteworthy.

text: In the first place, all the criticism of Stalin is directed at his actions subsequent to 1934; these are criticized, not because they were vile in themselves, but because they were injurious to the party and to loyal party members.
text_raw:
In  the  first  place,  all  the  criticism  of
Stalin  is  directed  at  his  actions  subsequent  to  1934;  these  are  criticized,  not  because  they
were  vile  in  themselves,  but  because  they  were  injurious  to  the  party  and  to  loyal  party
members.

text: Throughout this speech, as in everything else he did in this period, Khrushchev was working to strengthen the party.
text_raw:
Throughout  this  speech,  as  in  everything  else  he  did  in  this  period,  Khrushchev
was  working  to  strengthen  the  party.

text: Moreover, by directing his criticism at Stalin personally, he exculpated himself and the other Bolshevik survivors who were fully as guilty as Stalin was â€” guilty not merely because they acquiesced in Stalin's atrocities from fear, as Khrushchev admitted in the speech, but because they fully cooperated with him.
text_raw:
Moreover,  by  directing  his  criticism  at  Stalin
personally,  he  exculpated  himself  and  the  other  Bolshevik  survivors  who  were  fully  as
guilty  as  Stalin  was â€” guilty  not  merely  because  they  acquiesced  in  Stalin's  atrocities
from  fear,  as  Khrushchev  admitted  in  the  speech,  but  because  they  fully  cooperated  with
him.

text: A study of Khrushchev's own life shows that he supported Stalin's atrocities fully at the time, often anticipated them, benefitted personally from them, and egged Stalin on to greater ones.
text_raw:
A  study  of  Khrushchev's  own  life  shows  that  he  supported  Stalin's  atrocities  fully  at
the  time,  often  anticipated  them,  benefitted  personally  from  them,  and  egged  Stalin  on  to
greater  ones.

text: In fact, even as Khrushchev in his speech condemned Stalin's acts which caused the deaths of thousands in the party, he defended Stalin's acts which caused the deaths of millions in the country.
text_raw:
In  fact,  even  as  Khrushchev  in  his  speech  condemned  Stalin's  acts  which
caused  the  deaths  of  thousands  in  the  party,  he  defended  Stalin's  acts  which  caused  the
deaths  of  millions  in  the  country.

text: The fault was not merely with Stalin; it was with the system; and, even wider than that, it was with Russia.
text_raw:
The  fault  was  not  merely  with  Stalin;  it  was  with  the
system;  and,  even  wider  than  that,  it  was  with  Russia.

text: Any system of human life which is based on autocracy and authority, as Russian life has always been, will turn up sadistic monsters, as Russia has throughout its history, again and again.
text_raw:
Any  system  of  human  life  which  is
based  on  autocracy  and  authority,  as  Russian  life  has  always  been,  will  turn  up  sadistic
monsters,  as  Russia  has  throughout  its  history,  again  and  again.

text: And the more completely total and irresponsible power is concentrated in one man's hands, the more frequently will a monster of sadism be produced.
text_raw:
And  the  more  completely
total  and  irresponsible  power  is  concentrated  in  one  man's  hands,  the  more  frequently  will
a  monster  of  sadism  be  produced.

text: The very structure of Russian life on the authoritarian lines it had always possessed drove Khrushchev, as it had driven Stalin thirty years before, to concentrate all power in his own hands.
text_raw:
The  very  structure  of  Russian  life  on  the  authoritarian  lines  it  had  always  possessed
drove  Khrushchev,  as  it  had  driven  Stalin  thirty  years  before,  to  concentrate  all  power  in
his  own  hands.

text: Neither man could relax halfway to power for fear that someone else would continue on, seeking the peak of power.
text_raw:
Neither  man  could  relax  halfway  to  power  for  fear  that  someone  else
would  continue  on,  seeking  the  peak  of  power.

text: The basis of the whole system was fear and, like all neurotic drives in a neurotic system, such fear could not he overcome even by achievement of total power.
text_raw:
The  basis  of  the  whole  system  was  fear
and,  like  all  neurotic  drives  in  a  neurotic  system,  such  fear  could  not  he  overcome  even
by  achievement  of  total  power.

text: That is why it grows into paranoia as it did with Ivan the Terrible, Peter the Great, Paul I, Stalin, and others.
text_raw:
That  is  why  it  grows  into  paranoia  as  it  did  with  Ivan  the
Terrible,  Peter  the  Great,  Paul  I,  Stalin,  and  others.

text: During all the struggle for power within the Kremlin, foreign affairs were still actively pursued hy the Soviet leaders.
text_raw:
During  all  the  struggle  for  power  within  the  Kremlin,  foreign  affairs  were  still  actively
pursued  hy  the  Soviet  leaders.

text: The chief event was a change in direction from Europe to Asia which took place in the spring of 1955.
text_raw:
The  chief  event  was  a  change  in  direction  from  Europe  to
Asia  which  took  place  in  the  spring  of  1955.

text: The Austrian treaty, the reconciliation with Tito, the stalemate over the German problem, the Warsaw Pact, and the "Geneva spirit" were all parts of a plan to put Europe "on ice" in order to shift attention to Southeast Asia, to India, and to the Near East.
text_raw:
The  Austrian  treaty,  the  reconciliation  with
Tito,  the  stalemate  over  the  German  problem,  the  Warsaw  Pact,  and  the  "Geneva  spirit"
were  all  parts  of  a  plan  to  put  Europe  "on  ice"  in  order  to  shift  attention  to  Southeast
Asia,  to  India,  and  to  the  Near  East.

text: This new direction was opened by beginning arms shipments to Colonel Gamal Nasser of Egypt in the spring of 1955 and reached its peak in the so-called Suez Crisis of October 1956.
text_raw:
This  new  direction  was  opened  by  beginning  arms
shipments  to  Colonel  Gamal  Nasser  of  Egypt  in  the  spring  of  1955  and  reached  its  peak
in  the  so-called  Suez  Crisis  of  October  1956.

text: A similar effort in India, seeking to win its support for the Soviet bloc, began with the state visit to India and Burma by Bulganin and Khrushchev in November 1955.
text_raw:
A  similar  effort  in  India,  seeking  to  win  its
support  for  the  Soviet  bloc,  began  with  the  state  visit  to  India  and  Burma  by  Bulganin  and
Khrushchev  in  November  1955.

text: This new direction and its consequences will be described in a moment, but it must be recognized that the continuing struggle for control within the Kremlin and the satellite states ran parallel with the growing crisis in the Near East and that both reached the critical stage at the same time in October 956.
text_raw:
This  new  direction  and  its  consequences  will  be
described  in  a  moment,  but  it  must  be  recognized  that  the  continuing  struggle  for  control
within  the  Kremlin  and  the  satellite  states  ran  parallel  with  the  growing  crisis  in  the  Near
East  and  that  both  reached  the  critical  stage  at  the  same  time  in  October  956.

text: The struggle between the Stalinists and the anti-Stalinists within the satellite states and the discontent of the inhabitants with both groups kept public affairs agitated along the whole zone of satellite areas from the Baltic to the Balkans.
text_raw:
The  struggle  between  the  Stalinists  and  the  anti-Stalinists  within  the  satellite  states  and
the  discontent  of  the  inhabitants  with  both  groups  kept  public  affairs  agitated  along  the
whole  zone  of  satellite  areas  from  the  Baltic  to  the  Balkans.

text: Khrushchev's "secret speech" increased this agitation.
text_raw:
Khrushchev's  "secret  speech"
increased  this  agitation.

text: Pressure on Khrushchev inside the Kremlin to reverse his professed policy of de-Stalinization grew.
text_raw:
Pressure  on  Khrushchev  inside  the  Kremlin  to  reverse  his
professed  policy  of  de-Stalinization  grew.

text: Khrushchev struck back.
text_raw: Khrushchev  struck  back.

text: On June 2, 1956, the same day that Tito arrived for a state visit to Moscow, Molotov was removed as foreign minister and replaced by Khrushchev's agent, Shepilov, the editor of Pravda.

On  June  2,  1956,  the
same  day  that  Tito  arrived  for  a  state  visit  to  Moscow,  Molotov  was  removed  as  foreign
minister  and  replaced  by  Khrushchev's  agent,  Shepilov,  the  editor  of  Pravda.

text: But the satellite turmoil continued.
text_raw:
But  the
satellite  turmoil  continued.

text: This turmoil, which agitated eastern Europe for many years, may be regarded as a series of clashes between Stalinism and Titoism.
text_raw:
This  turmoil,  which  agitated  eastern  Europe  for  many  years,  may  be  regarded  as  a
series  of  clashes  between  Stalinism  and  Titoism.

text: Neither of these is an extreme pole of dualistic opposition but rather two positions on a number of scales, concerned rather with methods than with goals.
text_raw:
Neither  of  these  is  an  extreme  pole  of
dualistic  opposition  but  rather  two  positions  on  a  number  of  scales,  concerned  rather  with
methods  than  with  goals.

text: Both have as a goal the creation of powerful and prosperous
text_raw: Both  have  as  a  goal  the  creation  of  powerful  and  prosperous

text: Communist systems, but they do not agree on methods, or rather on the relative mixture of methods to be used to reach their goal.
text_raw:
Communist  systems,  but  they  do  not  agree  on  methods,  or  rather  on  the  relative  mixture
of  methods  to  be  used  to  reach  their  goal.

text: Each sees industrialization as necessary to such a goal, but Tito is, perhaps necessarily, more willing to use foreign investment and foreign technical guidance, if these are free from any political control.
text_raw:
Each  sees  industrialization  as  necessary  to  such
a  goal,  but  Tito  is,  perhaps  necessarily,  more  willing  to  use  foreign  investment  and
foreign  technical  guidance,  if  these  are  free  from  any  political  control.

text: Stalinism in general distrusts all foreign help as spying.
text_raw: Stalinism  in  general  distrusts  all  foreign  help  as  spying.

text: Relying on domestic capital accumulation, and determined to raise it speedily, Stalinism puts severe pressures on the peasantry and thus emphasizes collective farms under political pressure, while Titoism is prepared to make much more use of private agriculture and of economic incentives for food production.
text_raw:
Relying  on  domestic  capital
accumulation,  and  determined  to  raise  it  speedily,  Stalinism  puts  severe  pressures  on  the
peasantry  and  thus  emphasizes  collective  farms  under  political  pressure,  while  Titoism  is
prepared  to  make  much  more  use  of  private  agriculture  and  of  economic  incentives  for
food  production.

text: This entails a slower rate of industrialization and more emphasis on improved standards of living.
text_raw:
This  entails  a  slower  rate  of  industrialization  and  more  emphasis  on
improved  standards  of  living.

text: There are also other, more pervasive, differences.
text_raw: There  are  also  other,  more  pervasive,  differences.

text: Stalinism insists on uniformity and centralized authority, while Titoism is more willing to allow diversity and collegial control.
text_raw:
Stalinism
insists  on  uniformity  and  centralized  authority,  while  Titoism  is  more  willing  to  allow
diversity  and  collegial  control.

text: This, in their terms, is the distinction between a "monolithic block" and "collective leadership"; when the "monolithic bloc" is subject to criticism, it is called the "cult of personality."
text_raw:
This,  in  their  terms,  is  the  distinction  between  a
"monolithic  block"  and  "collective  leadership";  when  the  "monolithic  bloc"  is  subject  to
criticism,  it  is  called  the  "cult  of  personality."

text: In the satellites, for historical reasons, there are other sharp distinctions between Stalinism and Titoism.
text_raw:
In  the  satellites,  for  historical  reasons,  there  are  other  sharp  distinctions  between
Stalinism  and  Titoism.

text: The former favors Russian domination, while the latter favors local nationalism.
text_raw:
The  former  favors  Russian  domination,  while  the  latter  favors
local  nationalism.

text: As a consequence, in 1945-1960, the former favored those local leaders who had spent the prewar and war periods in exile in the Soviet Union, while the latter favored the underground fighters who had stayed at home in the Left-wing resistance groups.
text_raw:
As  a  consequence,  in  1945-1960,  the  former  favored  those  local
leaders  who  had  spent  the  prewar  and  war  periods  in  exile  in  the  Soviet  Union,  while  the
latter  favored  the  underground  fighters  who  had  stayed  at  home  in  the  Left-wing
resistance  groups.

text: And, finally, the Stalinists upheld their road to Socialism as the only road, while the Titoists contended there were many roads to Socialism.
text_raw:
And,  finally,  the  Stalinists  upheld  their  road  to  Socialism  as  the  only
road,  while  the  Titoists  contended  there  were  many  roads  to  Socialism.

text: As might be expected, political oppression and the rule of the monolithic party was associated with the one point of view, while a greater readiness to allow diversity of outlook and coalition regimes marked the other.
text_raw:
As  might  be
expected,  political  oppression  and  the  rule  of  the  monolithic  party  was  associated  with  the
one  point  of  view,  while  a  greater  readiness  to  allow  diversity  of  outlook  and  coalition
regimes  marked  the  other.

text: There is no doubt that Stalin intended to establish a fully Stalinist system as just described in eastern Europe, "the Zone," as Seton- Watson calls it.
text_raw:
There  is  no  doubt  that  Stalin  intended  to  establish  a  fully  Stalinist  system  as  just
described  in  eastern  Europe,  "the  Zone,"  as  Seton- Watson  calls  it.

text: But this could not be done immediately in the chaos of war's ending.
text_raw:
But  this  could  not  be
done  immediately  in  the  chaos  of  war's  ending.

text: Accordingly, a period of real coalition regimes was established, based on the association of all groups and parties which had resisted Nazism.
text_raw:
Accordingly,  a  period  of  real  coalition
regimes  was  established,  based  on  the  association  of  all  groups  and  parties  which  had
resisted  Nazism.

text: Most of these groups were made up of peasants, workers, and intellectuals led by a combination of exiles back from Russia and hardened resistance fighters.
text_raw:
Most  of  these  groups  were  made  up  of  peasants,  workers,  and
intellectuals  led  by  a  combination  of  exiles  back  from  Russia  and  hardened  resistance
fighters.

text: One of the chief acts of these coalition regimes, in most countries, was agrarian reform, that is, the division of former large estates into the hands of peasant owners.
text_raw:
One  of  the  chief  acts  of  these  coalition  regimes,  in  most  countries,  was  agrarian
reform,  that  is,  the  division  of  former  large  estates  into  the  hands  of  peasant  owners.

text: Within a few years, and in most cases by 1948, this coalition was broken down and replaced by narrow Stalinist control, governed by a typical Stalinist tyranny.
text_raw:
Within  a  few  years,  and  in  most  cases  by  1948,  this  coalition  was  broken  down  and
replaced  by  narrow  Stalinist  control,  governed  by  a  typical  Stalinist  tyranny.

text: This was achieved by getting the significant government posts into the hands of hard-core Stalinists, usually the former Moscow exiles, and forcing other groups out of the coalition.
text_raw:
This  was
achieved  by  getting  the  significant  government  posts  into  the  hands  of  hard-core
Stalinists,  usually  the  former  Moscow  exiles,  and  forcing  other  groups  out  of  the
coalition.

text: In this process, the presence of Soviet troops was often the vital factor.
text_raw: In  this  process,  the  presence  of  Soviet  troops  was  often  the  vital  factor.

text: Along with this went a social, economic, and propagandist campaign to split the farmers by calling the more affluent, better educated, or more obstinate ones "agrarian reactionaries" and "enemies of the people." These were liquidated, frequently by death.
text_raw:
Along
with  this  went  a  social,  economic,  and  propagandist  campaign  to  split  the  farmers  by
calling  the  more  affluent,  better  educated,  or  more  obstinate  ones  "agrarian  reactionaries"
and  "enemies  of  the  people."  These  were  liquidated,  frequently  by  death.

text: The chief index showing that this stage had been reached was usually a reversal of the agricultural policy from agrarian reform to collectivization similar to that achieved in Russia in 1930-1934.
text_raw:
The  chief  index
showing  that  this  stage  had  been  reached  was  usually  a  reversal  of  the  agricultural  policy
from  agrarian  reform  to  collectivization  similar  to  that  achieved  in  Russia  in  1930-1934.

text: As one consequence of this change, each satellite found its welfare, especially in economics, subordinated to that of the Soviet Union.
text_raw:
As  one  consequence  of  this  change,  each  satellite  found  its  welfare,  especially  in
economics,  subordinated  to  that  of  the  Soviet  Union.

text: This was reflected in numerous economic and commercial agreements which set up conditions of commercial exchange and joint-owned public corporations able to milk the satellite countries for Russia's benefit.
text_raw:
This  was  reflected  in  numerous
economic  and  commercial  agreements  which  set  up  conditions  of  commercial  exchange
and  joint-owned  public  corporations  able  to  milk  the  satellite  countries  for  Russia's
benefit.

text: Some of this was based on reparations.
text_raw: Some  of  this  was  based  on  reparations.

text: As examples of this exploitation, we might mention that the joint corporations in East Germany drained from that area goods worth a billion Reichsmarks a year in terms of 1936 prices in the 1946-1948 period.
text_raw:
As  examples  of  this  exploitation,  we
might  mention  that  the  joint  corporations  in  East  Germany  drained  from  that  area  goods
worth  a  billion  Reichsmarks  a  year  in  terms  of  1936  prices  in  the  1946-1948  period.

text: The Soviet- Polish coal agreement of 1945 bound Poland to sell coal to Russia at one-tenth the price obtainable elsewhere.
text_raw:
The
Soviet- Polish  coal  agreement  of  1945  bound  Poland  to  sell  coal  to  Russia  at  one-tenth  the
price  obtainable  elsewhere.

text: In all, it has been estimated that the Soviet Union extracted goods worth $20 billion out of eastern Europe in 1945-1946.
text_raw:
In  all,  it  has  been  estimated  that  the  Soviet  Union  extracted
goods  worth  $20  billion  out  of  eastern  Europe  in  1945-1946.

text: By 1952, eastern Europe, with the notable exception of Yugoslavia, was being organized, as a colony of the Soviet Union, along Stalinist lines.
text_raw:
By  1952,  eastern  Europe,  with  the  notable  exception  of  Yugoslavia,  was  being
organized,  as  a  colony  of  the  Soviet  Union,  along  Stalinist  lines.

text: The bitter attacks on Tito arose from Tito's refusal to accept this and from the challenge which the existence of his different system offered to Stalin's control.
text_raw:
The  bitter  attacks  on
Tito  arose  from  Tito's  refusal  to  accept  this  and  from  the  challenge  which  the  existence  of
his  different  system  offered  to  Stalin's  control.

text: Tito was able to resist because he was outside the zone of Soviet military occupation and had built up a military and bureaucratic hierarchy loyal to him, while inside that zone these hierarchies had been constructed under Soviet guidance and were loyal to Stalin rather than to the local leaders.
text_raw:
Tito  was  able  to  resist  because  he  was
outside  the  zone  of  Soviet  military  occupation  and  had  built  up  a  military  and
bureaucratic  hierarchy  loyal  to  him,  while  inside  that  zone  these  hierarchies  had  been
constructed  under  Soviet  guidance  and  were  loyal  to  Stalin  rather  than  to  the  local
leaders.

text: The one exception, Albania, sided with Stalin because it feared Yugoslavia, just as Tito feared the Soviet Union, as a too powerful neighbor.
text_raw:
The  one  exception,  Albania,  sided  with  Stalin  because  it  feared  Yugoslavia,  just
as  Tito  feared  the  Soviet  Union,  as  a  too  powerful  neighbor.

text: In 1951-1952 the incipient purge in the Soviet Union was extended to the satellites where its anti-Semitic overtones were even more evident.
text_raw:
In  1951-1952  the
incipient  purge  in  the  Soviet  Union  was  extended  to  the  satellites  where  its  anti-Semitic
overtones  were  even  more  evident.

text: Rudolf Slansky, leader of the Czech Communist Party, was tried and executed in spite of his abject subservience to Stalin, while Anna Pauker was removed from her offices in Romania.
text_raw:
Rudolf  Slansky,  leader  of  the  Czech  Communist
Party,  was  tried  and  executed  in  spite  of  his  abject  subservience  to  Stalin,  while  Anna
Pauker  was  removed  from  her  offices  in  Romania.

text: This drove Tito closer to the Western camp and led Tito's friend Milovan Djilas to recognize that the problem of Stalinism was not personal but institutional, caused by the structure of the system, a disease fatal to any real social welfare; he called this disease "bureaucratic degeneration." When Djilas went further, at the end of 1953, and recognized that the real issue was between freedom and absolutism, a choice for all the Zone between the West and the East, he broke with Tito because his criticism clearly applied to Tito's authoritarian bureaucracy as well.
text_raw:
This  drove  Tito  closer  to  the  Western
camp  and  led  Tito's  friend  Milovan  Djilas  to  recognize  that  the  problem  of  Stalinism  was
not  personal  but  institutional,  caused  by  the  structure  of  the  system,  a  disease  fatal  to  any
real  social  welfare;  he  called  this  disease  "bureaucratic  degeneration."  When  Djilas  went
further,  at  the  end  of  1953,  and  recognized  that  the  real  issue  was  between  freedom  and
absolutism,  a  choice  for  all  the  Zone  between  the  West  and  the  East,  he  broke  with  Tito
because  his  criticism  clearly  applied  to  Tito's  authoritarian  bureaucracy  as  well.

text: Many persons in the satellites, even the young who had lifelong indoctrination in the authoritarian outlook, reached similar conclusions and were like tinder to any anti-Soviet spark.
text_raw:
Many
persons  in  the  satellites,  even  the  young  who  had  lifelong  indoctrination  in  the
authoritarian  outlook,  reached  similar  conclusions  and  were  like  tinder  to  any  anti-Soviet
spark.

text: The sparks were provided by Khrushchev, with his continued curtailment of the secret police, his acceptance of Titoism, and, above all, his "secret speech." Few recognized that Khrushchev was basically an ultra- Stalinist himself, fully committed to foreign aggression, to ultra-industrialization, and to ruthless discipline of the working masses, especially the peasants.
text_raw:
The  sparks  were  provided  by  Khrushchev,  with  his  continued  curtailment  of  the  secret
police,  his  acceptance  of  Titoism,  and,  above  all,  his  "secret  speech."  Few  recognized  that
Khrushchev  was  basically  an  ultra- Stalinist  himself,  fully  committed  to  foreign
aggression,  to  ultra-industrialization,  and  to  ruthless  discipline  of  the  working  masses,
especially  the  peasants.

text: His tactical shifts were taken as indicators of a moderate personality, while, in fact, Khrushchev was as extreme as Stalin and more reckless.
text_raw:
His  tactical  shifts  were  taken  as  indicators  of  a  moderate
personality,  while,  in  fact,  Khrushchev  was  as  extreme  as  Stalin  and  more  reckless.

text: As part of the thaw in eastern Europe there was a considerable shift from Stalinism.
text_raw: As  part  of  the  thaw  in  eastern  Europe  there  was  a  considerable  shift  from  Stalinism.

text: Hundreds of thousands of political prisoners were either released or given reduced sentences, and party leaders who had been purged were restored to the party.
text_raw:
Hundreds  of  thousands  of  political  prisoners  were  either  released  or  given  reduced
sentences,  and  party  leaders  who  had  been  purged  were  restored  to  the  party.

text: Some who had been executed were posthumously rehabilitated.
text_raw:
Some  who
had  been  executed  were  posthumously  rehabilitated.

text: That key indicator, pressure to build
text_raw: That  key  indicator,  pressure  to  build

text: up collective farms, was reversed.
text_raw: up  collective  farms,  was  reversed.

text: In Hungary in a single year (May 1953 to May 1954) the acreage under collective farming decreased one-third, while the number of peasants on such farms fell 45 percent.
text_raw:
In  Hungary  in  a  single  year  (May  1953  to  May  1954)
the  acreage  under  collective  farming  decreased  one-third,  while  the  number  of  peasants
on  such  farms  fell  45  percent.

text: This was fairly typical of the Zone as a whole.
text_raw: This  was  fairly  typical  of  the  Zone  as  a  whole.

text: This general shift undoubtedly encouraged resistance to Soviet domination, a feeling which was greatly increased in 1956 by three other factors:
text_raw:
This  general  shift  undoubtedly  encouraged  resistance  to  Soviet  domination,  a  feeling
which  was  greatly  increased  in  1956  by  three  other  factors:

text: (1) the growing impoverishment of the Zone from Soviet exploitation, from the poor crops and food shortages of 1956, and from the equally grave fuel shortages (both coal and petroleum);
(2) the shift of Soviet attention from Europe to Asia;
text_raw: (2)  the  shift  of  Soviet  attention  from  Europe  to  Asia;

text: (3) the unexpected reaction to the "secret speech." The consequences of these disturbing influences were general in the Zone, but the specific cases of Poland and Hungary hold great interest, because they worked in such totally different ways.
text_raw:
(3)  the  unexpected  reaction  to  the
"secret  speech."  The  consequences  of  these  disturbing  influences  were  general  in  the
Zone,  but  the  specific  cases  of  Poland  and  Hungary  hold  great  interest,  because  they
worked  in  such  totally  different  ways.

text: The chief difference, of course, was the great strength of the Polish leaders and people, going back to their terrible experiences at the hands of troth Russians and Germans and their memories of the extraordinary feats of the underground resistance.
text_raw:
The  chief  difference,  of  course,  was  the  great  strength  of  the  Polish  leaders  and
people,  going  back  to  their  terrible  experiences  at  the  hands  of  troth  Russians  and
Germans  and  their  memories  of  the  extraordinary  feats  of  the  underground  resistance.

text: Soviet reactions to Polish demands for liberalizing the regime were undoubtedly influenced by a reluctance to meet that resistance again.
text_raw:
Soviet  reactions  to  Polish  demands  for  liberalizing  the  regime  were  undoubtedly
influenced  by  a  reluctance  to  meet  that  resistance  again.

text: However, the chief difference lay in the related fact that the leaders of the Polish Communist Party led the demand for liberalization and maintained a united front while doing so, while the Hungary movement was resisted by the party leaders and could be split by personal ambitions.
text_raw:
However,  the  chief  difference
lay  in  the  related  fact  that  the  leaders  of  the  Polish  Communist  Party  led  the  demand  for
liberalization  and  maintained  a  united  front  while  doing  so,  while  the  Hungary  movement
was  resisted  by  the  party  leaders  and  could  be  split  by  personal  ambitions.

text: The crisis began in both countries in the last week of June 1956.
text_raw: The  crisis  began  in  both  countries  in  the  last  week  of  June  1956.

text: A stoppage of work at the Polish railway factory in Poznan grew into a mass demonstration against the Communist regime.
text_raw:
A  stoppage  of  work
at  the  Polish  railway  factory  in  Poznan  grew  into  a  mass  demonstration  against  the
Communist  regime.

text: Shots were fired, and eventually over so were killed and 323 arrested.
text_raw:
Shots  were  fired,  and  eventually  over  so  were  killed  and  323
arrested.

text: Polish Party Secretary Ochab made concessions to the opposition and attributed the episode to "social roots . . . the existence of serious disturbances between the party and the various sections of the working class." This was rejected three days later by Bulganin during a sudden and unexpected visit of the Kremlin leaders to Warsaw; their version attributed the troubles to foreign capitalist agitators.
text_raw:
Polish  Party  Secretary  Ochab  made  concessions  to  the  opposition  and  attributed
the  episode  to  "social  roots  .  .  .  the  existence  of  serious  disturbances  between  the  party
and  the  various  sections  of  the  working  class."  This  was  rejected  three  days  later  by
Bulganin  during  a  sudden  and  unexpected  visit  of  the  Kremlin  leaders  to  Warsaw;  their
version  attributed  the  troubles  to  foreign  capitalist  agitators.

text: Ochab continued his concessions and, on August 4th, readmitted to the party the popular Vladislov Gomulka, a strong nationalist Communist who had been removed and imprisoned at Stalin's orders in 1951.
text_raw:
Ochab  continued  his
concessions  and,  on  August  4th,  readmitted  to  the  party  the  popular  Vladislov  Gomulka,
a  strong  nationalist  Communist  who  had  been  removed  and  imprisoned  at  Stalin's  orders
in  1951.

text: Because the continued worsening of economic conditions in the late summer of 1956 made it impossible for the Polish Communists to offer the people any substantial economic concessions, they continued the political relaxation, which alarmed the Kremlin.
text_raw:
Because  the  continued  worsening  of  economic  conditions  in  the  late  summer  of  1956
made  it  impossible  for  the  Polish  Communists  to  offer  the  people  any  substantial
economic  concessions,  they  continued  the  political  relaxation,  which  alarmed  the
Kremlin.

text: The trials of those arrested in the June disturbances were fair and punishments lenient, amid growing nationalist enthusiasm.
text_raw:
The  trials  of  those  arrested  in  the  June  disturbances  were  fair  and  punishments
lenient,  amid  growing  nationalist  enthusiasm.

text: On October 15th Moscow learned of a Polish decision to convene the Polish Central Committee on October 18th to elect a new Politburo which would not include Soviet Marshal K.
text_raw:
On  October  15th  Moscow  learned  of  a
Polish  decision  to  convene  the  Polish  Central  Committee  on  October  18th  to  elect  a  new
Politburo  which  would  not  include  Soviet  Marshal  K.

text: K.
text_raw: K.

Rokossovsky,  defense  minister
of  Poland  since  the  days  of  Stalin,  and  would  make  Gomulka  party  secretary.

text_raw:
After  a
hurried  meeting  of  the  Soviet  Presidium  on  October  18th,  Soviet  troops  and  naval
contingents  began  to  converge  on  Poland,  and  Khrushchev,  Molotov,  Kaganovich,  and

text: The presence of that rigid Stalinist Molotov, who had been dismissed as foreign secretary
text_raw: The  presence  of  that  rigid  Stalinist  Molotov,  who  had  been  dismissed  as  foreign  secretary

text: in June, was significant of the precarious decline of Khrushchev's position in the Kremlin.

in  June,  was  significant  of  the  precarious  decline  of  Khrushchev's  position  in  the
Kremlin.

text: Khrushchev, however, acted as Soviet spokesman at the session in the Belvedere Palace.
text_raw:
Khrushchev,  however,  acted  as  Soviet  spokesman  at  the  session  in  the
Belvedere  Palace.

text: He was violent and bellicose, calling Gomulka a "traitor" and threatening dire consequences if the old Politburo, including Rokossovsky, was not reinstated.
text_raw:
He  was  violent  and  bellicose,  calling  Gomulka  a  "traitor"  and
threatening  dire  consequences  if  the  old  Politburo,  including  Rokossovsky,  was  not
reinstated.

text: Ochab, still Polish secretary, was firm, and ordered the immediate halt of Soviet troop advances, or all negotiations would be ended and the Poles would take the consequences.
text_raw:
Ochab,  still  Polish  secretary,  was  firm,  and  ordered  the  immediate  halt  of
Soviet  troop  advances,  or  all  negotiations  would  be  ended  and  the  Poles  would  take  the

text: This meant resistance to the Russians by the tough, well-armed Polish Security Corps.
text_raw:
This  meant  resistance  to  the  Russians  by  the  tough,  well-armed  Polish
Security  Corps.

text: Khrushchev stopped his troop movements, the Russians withdrew, and the session of the Polish Central Committee finished its work, electing a new non-Soviet Politburo which excluded Rokossovsky and made Gomulka secretary.
text_raw:
Khrushchev  stopped  his  troop  movements,  the  Russians  withdrew,  and
the  session  of  the  Polish  Central  Committee  finished  its  work,  electing  a  new  non-Soviet
Politburo  which  excluded  Rokossovsky  and  made  Gomulka  secretary.

text: The latter in the course of the discussions with Khrushchev had indicated that his liberalization would extend only to domestic affairs and would not injure Polish-Soviet "friendship" or the Warsaw Pact.
text_raw:
The  latter  in  the
course  of  the  discussions  with  Khrushchev  had  indicated  that  his  liberalization  would
extend  only  to  domestic  affairs  and  would  not  injure  Polish-Soviet  "friendship"  or  the
Warsaw  Pact.

text: In his speech to the committee, Gomulka sought to reconcile nationalist Communism with Polish-Soviet friendship, and made a severe attack on the "cult of personality" with its hideous atrocities under the Stalinist regime.
text_raw:
In  his  speech  to  the  committee,  Gomulka  sought  to  reconcile  nationalist
Communism  with  Polish-Soviet  friendship,  and  made  a  severe  attack  on  the  "cult  of
personality"  with  its  hideous  atrocities  under  the  Stalinist  regime.

text: Rokossovsky resigned as defense minister and returned to Russia with more than thirty other Soviet high military officers in November.

Rokossovsky  resigned
as  defense  minister  and  returned  to  Russia  with  more  than  thirty  other  Soviet  high

text: Khrushchev publicly yielded in the Polish crisis on October 23rd when he issued a statement that he saw no obstacles to relations between the two countries from the committee's actions and that the Soviet troops would be withdrawn to their bases.
text_raw:
Khrushchev  publicly  yielded  in  the  Polish  crisis  on  October  23rd  when  he  issued  a

committee's  actions  and  that  the  Soviet  troops  would  be  withdrawn  to  their  bases.

text: On the same day, he was taking steps to crush the parallel crisis in Hungary.
text_raw:
On  the
same  day,  he  was  taking  steps  to  crush  the  parallel  crisis  in  Hungary.

text: The troubles in the Magyar state in the summer of 1956 took the same forms as in Poland, but instead of being directed by the Communist party secretary, they were directed against him.
